Great Chapter 1.1.
Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā)
1.1.1. Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in What is Heard (Sutamayañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom regarding the application of the ear is knowledge consisting in what is heard?
The application of the ear is [the thought]: "These phenomena are to be directly known. The wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“The application of the ear [to the thought], ‘These phenomena are to be fully understood’—the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
The application of the ear [to the thought], ‘These phenomena are to be abandoned’—the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
The application of the ear [to the thought], ‘These phenomena are to be developed’—the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.”
“The application of the ear [to the thought], ‘These phenomena are to be realized’; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard (sutamaye ñāṇaṃ).
“The application of the ear [to the thought], ‘These phenomena lead to decline’; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“The application of the ear [to the thought], ‘These phenomena lead to stability’; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.”
“‘These phenomena partake of distinction’—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
‘These phenomena partake of penetration’—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.”
“All conditioned phenomena are suffering”: this is the ear-opening; the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“All phenomena are non-self”: this is the ear-opening; the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“This is the noble truth of suffering”: this is the ear-opening; the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“The noble truth of the origin of suffering”—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“The noble truth of the cessation of suffering”—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
“The noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering”—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
How is it that the application of the ear [to the thought], “These phenomena are to be directly known,” and the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard?

purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction is to be directly known;
purification of view in the sense of seeing is to be directly known.
Liberation is to be directly known in the sense of being released;
true knowledge is to be directly known in the sense of penetration;
deliverance is to be directly known in the sense of relinquishment.

[8] Will is to be directly known in the sense of being the root.
Attention is to be directly known in the sense of origination;
contact is to be directly known in the sense of convergence;
feeling is to be directly known in the sense of meeting place.

mindfulness is to be directly known in the sense of being the dominant influence;
wisdom is to be directly known in the sense of being supreme.
Liberation is to be directly known in the sense of its essence;
Nibbāna, which plunges into the deathless, is to be directly known in the sense of its consummation.
Whatever phenomena are directly known, those phenomena are known.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.

How is it that "these states are to be fully understood" is the application of the ear, and the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard?
One thing to be fully understood:
contact that is accompanied by taints and conducive to clinging.
Two things to be fully understood:
Name-and-form.
Three things are to be fully understood:
the three feelings.
Four things are to be fully understood:
the four nutriments.

The five aggregates of clinging.

the six internal sense bases.

The eight worldly conditions.

the nine abodes of beings.
Ten things are to be fully understood:
the ten bases.

forms are to be fully understood;

the mind is to be fully understood;
mental phenomena are to be fully understood.
Mind-consciousness is to be fully understood;
mind-contact is to be fully understood;
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is to be fully understood.”
Form is to be fully understood;
feeling is to be fully understood;
perception is to be fully understood.

Formations are to be fully understood; consciousness is to be fully understood; the eye is to be fully understood... [and so on] ... The requested output is: Formations are to be fully understood; consciousness is to be fully understood; the eye is to be fully understood... [and so on] ...
Old age and death are to be fully understood; ...pe...
Nibbāna, which plunges into the deathless, is to be fully understood in the sense of being the ultimate goal.
When those various states for the sake of whose attainment one exerts effort are actually attained, then those states are both fully understood and definitively determined.
For one striving for the attainment of renunciation, renunciation is attained.
In this way, that state is both fully understood and scrutinized.
For one striving for the attainment of non-ill will, non-ill will is attained.
In this way, that Dhamma is both fully understood and scrutinized.
For one striving for the attainment of the perception of light, the perception of light is attained.
In this way, that Dhamma is both fully understood and scrutinized.
For one striving for the attainment of non-distraction, non-distraction is attained.
In this way, that phenomenon (dhamma) is both fully understood and scrutinized.
For one striving for the attainment of the determination of phenomena, the determination of phenomena is attained.
In this way, that phenomenon is both fully understood and scrutinized.
For one striving to attain knowledge, knowledge is attained.
In this way, that phenomenon is both fully understood and scrutinized.
For one striving for the sake of attaining gladness, gladness is attained.
In this way, that state is both fully understood and scrutinized.
[7] For one striving for the sake of attaining the first jhāna, the first jhāna is attained.
In this way, that phenomenon is both fully understood and scrutinized.
[The same applies to] the second jhāna … the third jhāna …

In this way, that phenomenon is both fully understood and scrutinized.

For one striving for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is acquired.

[8] For one who exerts effort for the sake of attaining the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of impermanence is attained.

For one striving for the attainment of the contemplation of dispassion (*virāgānupassanā*), the contemplation of dispassion is attained.
In this way, that state (*dhamma*) is both fully understood and scrutinized.

In the sense of knowing, that is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“‘These states are to be fully understood’—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
[2] The Exposition of What is to be Fully Understood.
How is it that the application of the ear [to the thought], “These phenomena are to be abandoned,” and the wisdom that understands this, is knowledge consisting in what is heard?
One phenomenon is to be abandoned:
the conceit “I am.”
Two things are to be abandoned:
ignorance and craving for existence.
Three things are to be abandoned:
There are three cravings.
There are four things to be abandoned—
the four floods.
Five things are to be abandoned—
the five hindrances.
Six things are to be abandoned—
Six groups of craving.
Seven things to be abandoned—
the seven underlying tendencies.
Eight things are to be abandoned—
the eight wrongnesses.
Nine things are to be abandoned—
Nine things rooted in craving.
Ten states to be abandoned:
the ten wrongnesses.
There are two kinds of abandoning:
abandoning by eradication and abandoning by subsiding.
Abandoning by eradication belongs to one who develops the supramundane path leading to the destruction [of defilements].
And the abandoning by subsiding occurs at the moment of the fruit.
There are three kinds of abandoning:
"The escape from sensual desires is this, namely, renunciation."
This is the escape from forms, namely, the formless;
and whatever is become, conditioned, and dependently arisen, its cessation is the escape.
For one who has attained renunciation, sensual desires are both abandoned and relinquished.
For one who has attained the formless, forms are both abandoned and relinquished.
For one who has attained cessation, mental formations are both abandoned and relinquished.
Regarding the four abandonments: while penetrating the penetration of full understanding, one abandons the truth of suffering.
While penetrating the penetration of abandoning, one abandons the truth of the origin;
while penetrating the penetration of realization, one abandons the truth of cessation;
while penetrating the penetration of development, one abandons the truth of the path.
There are five abandonings:
abandoning by suppression, abandoning by substitution of opposites, abandoning by cutting off, abandoning by tranquillization, and abandoning by escape.
Abandoning by suppression is the abandoning of the hindrances for one developing the first jhāna.
The abandoning as a factor is for one developing concentration partaking of penetration;
the abandoning by cutting off is for one developing the supramundane path leading to the destruction [of defilements];
and the abandoning by subsiding is at the moment of the fruit.
Abandonment as escape is cessation, which is Nibbāna.
“Monks, everything is to be abandoned.
And what, monks, is everything that is to be abandoned?”
The eye, monks, is to be abandoned;
forms are to be abandoned;
eye-consciousness is to be abandoned.
Eye-contact is to be abandoned;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be abandoned.
The ear is to be abandoned.
Sounds are to be abandoned … [and so on] … the nose is to be abandoned;
odors are to be abandoned …
The tongue is to be abandoned;
tastes are to be abandoned;
… the body is to be abandoned.
Tangible objects are to be abandoned… the mind is to be abandoned;
mental phenomena are to be abandoned…
“Mind-consciousness is to be abandoned;
mind-contact is to be abandoned;
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is to be abandoned.”

Seeing form, one abandons it; seeing feeling, one abandons it; seeing perception, one abandons it; seeing volitional formations, one abandons them; seeing consciousness, one abandons it. Seeing the eye … [and so on] … seeing aging-and-death … [and so on].
Seeing Nibbāna, which is plunged into the deathless, as the ultimate goal, one abandons.
Whatever states have been abandoned, those very states are relinquished.
That is knowledge (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom (*paññā*) in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
“The application of the ear that ‘these states are to be abandoned’; the understanding of that is wisdom consisting in knowledge of what consists in the heard.
[3] The third recitation section.
How is it that the application of the ear [thinking], “These states are to be developed,” and the understanding consisting in the discernment thereof is knowledge consisting in what is heard?
One state is to be developed:
mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by pleasure.
Two things are to be developed:
serenity and insight.
Three things are to be developed:
Three concentrations.
Four things to be developed—
the four foundations of mindfulness.
Five things are to be developed:
the five-factored concentration.
Six things are to be developed:
The six bases for recollection.
Seven things to be developed—
the seven factors of enlightenment.
Eight things are to be developed:
the Noble Eightfold Path.
Nine things are to be developed:
The nine factors of striving for complete purity.
Ten things to be developed:
the ten kasiṇa bases.
There are two kinds of development:
mundane development and supramundane development.
There are three kinds of development:

The development of wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material sphere; the development of wholesome states pertaining to the immaterial sphere; and the development of wholesome states that are unincluded.
Regarding the development of wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material sphere, there is the inferior, the intermediate, and the superior.
Regarding the development of wholesome states pertaining to the immaterial sphere, there is the inferior, the intermediate, and the superior.
The development of wholesome states that are not included within the mundane is sublime.
There are four kinds of development:
one develops while penetrating the truth of suffering through the penetration of full understanding; [one develops] while penetrating the truth of the origin through the penetration of abandoning...
One develops while penetrating; one develops while penetrating the penetration of realization regarding the truth of cessation;
one develops while penetrating the penetration of cultivation regarding the truth of the path.
These are the four kinds of development. [4]
There are also four kinds of development:
development by seeking, development by acquisition, development by single flavor, and development by cultivation.
What is development by seeking?
For all those entering into concentration, the states arisen therein become of a single flavor;
this is development by seeking.
What is development by acquisition?
In all those who have attained concentration, the states born therein do not exceed one another;
this is development by acquisition.
What is development of single flavor?
For one developing the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution, the four faculties become of a single flavor by way of the faculty of faith;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties.
For one developing the faculty of energy in the sense of exertion, the four faculties become of a single flavor by way of the faculty of energy; thus...
Development is in the sense of the faculties having a single flavor.
For one developing the mindfulness faculty in the sense of establishing, the four faculties become of a single flavor by way of the mindfulness faculty;
thus, development is in the sense of the faculties having a single flavor.
For one developing the faculty of concentration in the sense of non-distraction, the four faculties become of a single flavor by means of the faculty of concentration;
this is development in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties.

For one developing the faculty of wisdom in the sense of seeing, the four faculties become of a single flavor by means of the faculty of wisdom; this is development in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties.
Development is in the sense of single flavor regarding the faculties.
For one developing the power of faith in the sense of being unshakable by lack of faith, the four powers become of a single flavor through the influence of the power of faith;
thus, development is in the sense of single flavor regarding the powers.
For one developing the power of energy in the sense of being unshakable by indolence, the four powers become of a single flavor through the influence of the power of energy;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the powers.
For one developing the power of mindfulness in the sense of being unshakable by negligence, the four powers become of a single flavor through the influence of the power of mindfulness; thus...
Development by way of the single flavor of the powers:
for one developing the concentration power in the sense of unshakability by restlessness, the four powers become of a single flavor through the influence of the concentration power;
thus it is development by way of the single flavor of the powers.
For one developing the power of wisdom in the sense of being unshakable by ignorance, the four powers become of a single flavor through the influence of the power of wisdom;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the powers.

For one developing the mindfulness enlightenment factor in the sense of establishing, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor through the influence of the mindfulness enlightenment factor; thus, [development is in the sense of their single flavor].
Development by way of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors:

for one developing the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor in the sense of investigating, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor through the influence of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor;
thus it is development by way of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors.
For one developing the energy enlightenment factor in the sense of exertion, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor by way of the energy enlightenment factor—
this is development in the sense of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors.

For one developing the rapture enlightenment factor in the sense of pervasion, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor by way of the rapture enlightenment factor— this is development in the sense of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors.
Development by way of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors:
for one developing the tranquility enlightenment factor in the sense of peace, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor through the influence of the tranquility enlightenment factor;
thus it is development by way of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors.
For one developing the concentration enlightenment factor in the sense of non-distraction, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor by way of the concentration enlightenment factor;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the enlightenment factors.

For one developing the equanimity enlightenment factor in the sense of reflexive consideration, the six enlightenment factors become of a single flavor by way of the equanimity enlightenment factor; thus...
Development in the sense of single flavor regarding the factors of enlightenment:
for one developing right view in the sense of seeing, the seven path-factors become of a single flavor by way of right view;
thus there is development in the sense of single flavor regarding the path-factors.
For one developing right intention in the sense of directing onto [the object], by way of right intention the seven path factors become of a single flavor;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the path factors.
For one developing right speech in the sense of embracing, by way of right speech the seven path factors become of a single flavor; thus...
Development is in the sense of a single flavor of the path factors.
For one developing right action in the sense of its origination, the seven path factors become of a single flavor by way of right action;
thus, development is in the sense of a single flavor of the path factors.
For one developing right livelihood in the sense of cleansing, the seven path factors become of a single flavor by way of right livelihood;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the path factors.
For one developing right effort in the sense of exertion, the seven path factors become of a single flavor by way of right effort; thus...
Development in the sense of single flavor of the path factors:
for one developing right mindfulness in the sense of establishing, the seven path factors become of a single flavor by way of right mindfulness;
thus it is development in the sense of single flavor of the path factors.
For one developing right concentration in the sense of non-distraction, the seven path factors become of a single flavor by way of right concentration;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the path factors.
This is development as a single flavor.
What is cultivation by way of repetition?
Here, a bhikkhu repeats [the practice] in the morning, he repeats it at midday, he repeats it in the evening;
he repeats it before the meal, he repeats it after the meal; he repeats it in the first watch of the night, and also in the middle watch...
One practices during the first watch, one practices during the last watch; one practices by night, one practices by day, and one practices both by night and by day;
one practices in the dark fortnight, one practices in the bright fortnight, one practices in the rainy season, one practices in the winter, and one practices in the summer;
one practices during the first stage of life, one practices during the middle stage of life, and one practices during the final stage of life.
One cultivates the aggregate of vitality— this is cultivation by way of repetition.
These are the four types of cultivation.
There are another four kinds of development:

development in the sense of non-excess of the states arisen therein; development in the sense of single function of the faculties; development in the sense of driving out the appropriate energy; development in the sense of repetition.
How is there development in the sense of non-excess of the states arisen therein?
For one abandoning sensual desire, the states born by way of renunciation do not overstep one another;
thus, in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states born therein, there is development.
For one abandoning ill will, the states born by way of non-ill will do not overstep one another... [and so on].
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of states arisen therein.
For one abandoning sloth and torpor by means of the perception of light, the states arisen do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of states arisen therein.
For one abandoning restlessness, the states arisen by way of non-distraction do not overstep one another;
thus, in that regard, development is in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning doubt, the states arisen by way of the definition of phenomena do not overstep one another; thus—
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states born therein.
For one abandoning ignorance by means of knowledge, the states born therein do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states born therein.
For one abandoning aversion, the states born by way of gladness do not overstep one another;
thus, in that regard, development is in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states born therein.
For one abandoning the hindrances, the states born by way of the first jhāna do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of non-excess of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning applied thought and sustained thought by means of the second jhāna, the states arisen therein do not exceed one another;
thus, development is in the sense of non-excess of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning rapture, the states born by way of the third jhāna do not exceed one another;
thus, in that regard, development is in the sense of the non-excess of states born therein.
For one abandoning pleasure and pain, the states born by way of the fourth jhāna do not exceed one another; thus—
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of states arisen therein.
For one who abandons perception of form, perception of resistance, and perception of diversity, the states arisen by way of the attainment of the base of infinite space do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of states arisen therein.
For one abandoning the perception of the base of infinite space, the states born by way of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness do not overstep one another;
thus, development in that regard is in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states born therein.
For one abandoning the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, the states born by way of the attainment of the base of nothingness do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning the perception of the base of nothingness, the states arisen by way of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning the perception of permanence, the states arisen by way of the contemplation of impermanence do not overstep one another;
thus, in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein, there is development (*bhāvanā*).
For one abandoning the perception of pleasure, the states arisen by way of the contemplation of suffering do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one who abandons the perception of self by means of the contemplation of non-self, the states arisen therein do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning delight, the states arisen by way of contemplation of disenchantment do not overstep one another;
thus, in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein, there is development.
For one abandoning lust, the states arisen by way of contemplation of dispassion do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of phenomena arisen therein.
For one who abandons origination by way of the contemplation of cessation, the phenomena arisen therein do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of phenomena arisen therein.
For one abandoning grasping, the states arisen by way of the contemplation of relinquishment do not overstep one another;
thus, in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein, there is development (*bhāvanā*).
For one abandoning the perception of compactness, the states arisen by way of the contemplation of destruction do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of phenomena arisen therein.
For one who abandons accumulation, by way of contemplation of fall, phenomena arisen therein do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of phenomena arisen therein.
For one abandoning the perception of permanence, the states arisen by way of contemplation of change do not overstep one another;
thus, in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein, there is development.
For one abandoning the sign, the states arisen by way of contemplation of the signless do not overstep one another.

Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein. For one abandoning aspiration, the states arisen by way of the contemplation of the wishless do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning misapprehension, the states arisen by way of the contemplation of emptiness do not transgress one another; thus...
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.

For one who abandons adherence by grasping at the core, the states arisen through the means of insight into phenomena (*dhamma-vipassanā*) under the heading of higher wisdom do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning adherence through delusion, the states arisen by way of knowledge and vision according to reality do not overstep one another;
thus, in that regard, development is in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning adherence through attachment, the states arisen by way of contemplation of danger do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one who abandons lack of reflection by means of the contemplation of reflection, the states arisen therein do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning adherence to bondage by way of contemplation of turning away, the states arisen do not overstep one another;
thus, in that regard, development is in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning defilements associated with views by way of the stream-entry path, the states arisen do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
For one abandoning gross defilements by means of the once-return path, the states arisen therein do not transgress one another;
thus, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
When one abandons defilements that have entered along with the underlying tendencies, the states arisen by way of the non-return path do not overstep one another;
thus, in the sense of the non-overstepping of the states arisen therein, there is development (bhāvanā).
When one abandons all defilements, the states arisen by way of the path of arahantship do not overstep one another.
Therein, development is in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
Thus is development in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein.
How is there development in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties?
For one abandoning sensual desire through the means of renunciation, the five faculties become of a single flavor;
thus, development is in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties.
For one abandoning ill will through the means of non-ill will, the five faculties become of a single flavor... [and so on].
Development of the faculties in the sense of their having a single function:
… [as before] … for one abandoning all defilements by means of the path of arahantship, the five faculties have a single function;
thus there is development of the faculties in the sense of their having a single function.
Thus is development in the sense of the faculties having a single function.
How is there development in the sense of driving the energy that has reached that [state]?
One who abandons sensual desire drives the energy by means of renunciation; thus it is development.
It is development in the sense of conveying energy that is conducive to it;
for when one abandons ill will, energy conveys [the mind] by way of non-ill will—thus it is development in the sense of conveying energy that is conducive to it... [and so on].
For one who abandons all defilements, energy is carried forward by means of the path of arahantship;

thus, it is development in the sense of carrying forward that energy which has approached that [state]. In this way, it is development in the sense of carrying forward that energy which has approached that [state].
How is it development in the sense of repeated practice?
One who abandons sensual desire practices renunciation;
thus it is development in the sense of repeated practice.
"Abandoning ill will, one cultivates non-ill will"—
this is development in the sense of cultivation. …pe… "Abandoning all defilements, one cultivates the path of arahantship"— this is development in the sense of cultivation.
Development in the sense of repeated practice.
Thus there is development in the sense of repeated practice.

These are the four kinds of development: one develops while seeing form; one develops while seeing feeling; one develops while seeing perception; one develops while seeing formations; one develops while seeing consciousness; [and] the eye … [and so on].
He develops [the path] while seeing aging-and-death … down to … Nibbāna, which plunges into the deathless,
as its consummation. Whatever states have been developed, those states become of a single flavor.
In the sense of being known, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"The application of the ear that 'these states are to be developed,' and the understanding of that, is wisdom; this is knowledge consisting in what is heard. [4]
The Exposition of What Is to Be Developed.
The Fourth Recitation Section.
How is it that the application of the ear [to the thought], “These phenomena are to be realized,” and the wisdom that understands that, is knowledge consisting in what is heard?
One thing is to be realized:
unshakable liberation of mind.
Two things are to be realized:
Knowledge and liberation.
Three things to be realized:
the three types of clear knowledge.
Four things are to be realized—
the four fruits of asceticism.
Five things are to be realized—
The five aggregates of Dhamma.
Six things to be realized—
the six direct knowledges.
Seven things are to be realized—
the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed.
Eight things are to be realized—
The eight liberations.
Nine things to be realized—
the nine successive cessations.
Ten things are to be realized—
the ten qualities of one beyond training.
"Monks, everything is to be realized."
And what, monks, is all that is to be realized?
The eye, monks, is to be realized;
forms are to be realized.
Eye-consciousness is to be realized;
eye-contact is to be realized;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be realized.
The ear is to be realized;
sounds are to be realized ... [and so on] ...
the nose is to be realized;
Odors are to be realized… the tongue is to be realized;
tastes are to be realized…
The body is to be realized;
tangibles are to be realized;
the mind is to be realized.
Phenomena are to be realized;
mind-consciousness is to be realized;
mind-contact is to be realized.
“Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too must be realized.
One realizes it while seeing form;
one realizes it while seeing feeling.
Contemplating perception, one realizes it;
contemplating mental formations, one realizes them;
contemplating consciousness, one realizes it.
Seeing the eye...
[and so on] ... aging-and-death...
[and so on] ... as having the Deathless, Nibbāna, as its culmination in the sense of being the ultimate end, he realizes it.
Whatever states have been realized, those very states have been touched.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:
“‘These states are to be realized’—the application of the ear [to this], and the wisdom that understands it, is knowledge consisting in what is heard.

How is it that “‘These states lead to decline, these states lead to stability, these states lead to distinction, these states lead to penetration’—the application of the ear [to this], and the wisdom that understands it, is knowledge consisting in what is heard”?
When one who has attained the first jhāna is assailed by perceptions and mental engagements associated with sensual desire...
A state conducive to decline.
Mindfulness in accordance with that state remains steady—
a state conducive to stability.
When perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by non-discursive thought prevail,
this is a state conducive to distinction.
When perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion prevail—
A state conducive to penetration.
When perception and attention accompanied by applied thought (vitakka) occur to one who has attained the second jhāna—
that is a state conducive to decline.
Mindfulness abides in accordance with that state—
this is a phenomenon partaking of stability.
Perception and attention accompanied by equanimity and pleasure manifest.
A state partaking of distinction.
When perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion are active,
it is a state partaking of penetration.
When perceptions and mental applications accompanied by rapture and pleasure still occur in one who has attained the third jhāna,
this is a state conducive to decline.
When mindfulness consistent with that state remains established, it is a state conducive to stability.
A state conducive to stability.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by neither-pain-nor-pleasure occur,
it is a state conducive to distinction.
When perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion occur,
that is a state partaking of penetration.
When perception and attention accompanied by equanimity occur for one who has attained the fourth jhāna—
A state conducive to decline.
Mindfulness that accords with that state remains steady—
a state conducive to stability.
When perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite space arise,
it is a state partaking of distinction.
When perceptions and mental engagements associated with disenchantment and accompanied by dispassion arise...
A state conducive to penetration.
For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the application of perception accompanied by forms occurs—
this is a state conducive to decline.
Mindfulness remains in accordance with that state—
this is a phenomenon partaking of stability.
Perception and attention accompanied by the base of infinite consciousness become manifest.
A state conducive to distinction.
When perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion are exercised,
it is a state conducive to penetration.
When perception and attention accompanied by the base of infinite space occur in one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness,
this is a state conducive to decline.
When mindfulness in accordance with that state becomes established, [this is a state conducive to distinction].
A state conducive to stability.
When perception and attention accompanied by the base of nothingness are active—
that is a state conducive to distinction.
When perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion occur,
that is a state conducive to penetration.
When for one who has attained the base of nothingness, perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by the base of infinite consciousness occur—
A state conducive to decline.
Mindfulness that conforms to that [state] remains steady—
a state conducive to stability.
Perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arise—
this is a state conducive to distinction.
Perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion arise— this is a state conducive to penetration.
The state conducive to penetration.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:

“‘These states lead to decline; these states lead to stability; these states lead to distinction; these states lead to penetration’—the act of attending to this is the ear, and the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.

How is it that “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are non-self”—the act of attending to this is the ear, and the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard?

“‘Form is impermanent in the sense of being subject to destruction; it is suffering in the sense of being fearful; it is non-self in the sense of being coreless’—the act of attending to this is the ear, and the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard.”
“Feeling … perception … volitional formations …”

“Consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … aging-and-death is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness”— this is the lending of the ear; the wisdom that understands this is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
In the sense of being known, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:

"All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are non-self"—this is the application of the ear, and the understanding thereof is wisdom, which is knowledge consisting in what is heard.

How is it that the ear is applied thus: "This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering"?
The wisdom that understands that is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
Therein, what is the noble truth of suffering?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering;
association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, and not to obtain what one desires is also suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Therein, what is birth?

It is the birth, the being born, the descent, the manifestation, the appearance of the aggregates, and the acquisition of the sense-bases of those various beings in their respective classes of beings.
This is called birth.

Therein, what is aging? That which, for various beings in their respective classes of beings, is aging, decrepitude, brokenness, graying of hair, wrinkling of skin, the decline of the life-span, and the maturation of the faculties—this is called aging.
In this context, what is death?

That which for various beings is the passing away from their respective classes of beings, the dissolution, the disappearance, death, dying, the completion of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, and the cutting off of the life-faculty— this is called death.
In this context, what is sorrow?
It is the sorrow of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by the loss of health,
or afflicted by the loss of virtue, or afflicted by the loss of view, or by some other such misfortune.
For one who is possessed [of these] and touched by some kind of painful state, there is sorrow, grieving, the state of being grieved,
inner sorrow, inner anguish, a burning of the mind, mental distress,
and the dart of sorrow— this is called sorrow.
In this context, what is lamentation?
It is the lamentation of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by the loss of health,
or afflicted by the loss of virtue, or afflicted by the loss of views, or by some other such misfortune.
For one who is possessed of this [body] and is touched by this or that painful state, there is weeping, lamentation, the act of weeping, the act of lamenting,
the state of having wept, the state of having lamented, verbal babble, prattle, wailing, the act of wailing, and the state of having wailed—
this is called lamentation (*parideva*).
In this context, what is suffering?
Whatever is bodily discomfort, bodily pain, the uncomfortable and painful feeling born of body-contact, the uncomfortable and painful sensation born of body-contact—
this is called suffering.
In this context, what is grief (*domanassa*)?
That which is mental unease, mental suffering, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of mental contact—
this is called grief.
In this context, what is despair?
It is the state of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by the loss of health,
or afflicted by the loss of virtue, or afflicted by the loss of right view, or by some other such misfortune.
For one who is possessed [of these] and touched by this or that state of suffering, there is striving, despairing,
the state of striving, the state of despairing, the quality of having striven, the quality of having despaired—
this is called despair (*upāyāsa*).
In this context, what is association with the unpleasant as suffering?
Here, there are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable to one;
or there are those who wish one harm, wish one ill, wish one discomfort, and wish one lack of security from bondage. Whatever [association] one has with them—
Association, meeting, conjunction, and mingling with those who are dear—
this is called the suffering of union with the unpleasant.
In this context, what is the suffering of separation from the pleasant?
Here, whatever forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tactile objects one finds desirable, lovely, and agreeable; or whoever are one's well-wishers,
those who desire one's welfare, one's comfort, and one's security from bondage— whether mother, father, brother,
sister, friend, colleague, kinsman, or blood relative— the lack of association, lack of meeting, lack of encounter, and lack of mingling with them.
This is called suffering due to separation from the beloved.
In this context, what is "not to get what one desires" as suffering?
For beings subject to birth, such a desire arises: [“O, that we were not subject to birth!”]
“O, that we were not subject to birth! O, that birth would not come to us!
Yet this cannot be attained by mere wishing;
thus, not getting what one wishes for is also suffering.
Of beings subject to aging …pe… of beings subject to illness … of beings subject to death …
In beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, such a wish arises:
"O, that we were not subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; that sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not come upon us!
Yet this cannot be attained by mere wishing.
This too is suffering: not to obtain what one desires.
In this regard, what are the five aggregates of clinging, in brief, that are suffering?
They are as follows:

The aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness— these, in brief,
are called the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering.
This is called the noble truth of suffering.
In this context, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Now, where does this craving arise when it arises, and where does it settle when it settles?
Whatever in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature—therein this craving, when arising, arises; therein, when settling, settles.
And what in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature?
The eye in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature; therein this craving, when arising, arises; therein, when settling, settles.
The ear in the world … the nose in the world … the tongue in the world … [and so on] … the mind in the world.
The body is dear and pleasant in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles. The mind is dear and pleasant in the world;
herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles. Visible forms are dear and pleasant in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
In the world, sounds are a lovely thing, a pleasant thing … mental phenomena in the world … eye-consciousness in the world … [and so forth].
Mental consciousness in the world … eye-contact in the world … [and so on] … mind-contact in the world …
In the world, feeling born of eye-contact … pe … feeling born of mind-contact … perception of forms in the world … pe …
Perception of mental phenomena in the world … volition regarding forms in the world … [and so on] … volition regarding mental phenomena in the world …
Craving for forms in the world … craving for mental phenomena in the world … thought directed toward forms in the world … [and so forth] … thought directed toward mental phenomena in the world.
Reflection on mental phenomena in the world...
investigation of forms in the world...
[and so on] ...investigation of mental phenomena in the world is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
In this regard, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving—its relinquishing, its renouncing, its liberation, and its non-attachment. Furthermore, where is that craving abandoned when it is being abandoned, and where does it cease when it is ceasing?
Whatever in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature—it is therein that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, when ceasing, it ceases.
And what in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature?
The eye in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature—it is therein that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, when ceasing, it ceases. …pe…
Investigation of phenomena is a state of endearment and gratification in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, it ceases.
This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering?
This indeed is the Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?
Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—
this is called right view.
In this context, what is right intention?
The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty—
this is called right intention.
In that regard, what is right speech?
Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter—
this is called right speech.
In this context, what is right action?
Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct—
this is called right action.
In this context, what is right livelihood?
Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by right livelihood—
this is called right livelihood.
In this context, what is right effort?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
[and he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives] for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states... [as before].

One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... [and so on] ...for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states—
this is called right effort.
Therein, what is right mindfulness?
Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
[He dwells] in relation to feelings ... [and so on].
He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind ... and contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—
this is called right mindfulness.
In this regard, what is right concentration?

Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who has equanimity and is mindful dwells happily. Thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
This is called right concentration.
This is called the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering;
this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—this is the application of the ear, and the understanding thereof.
Wisdom regarding what consists of the heard is knowledge.
Thus, wisdom regarding the application of the ear is knowledge consisting of what has been heard.
This is the first exposition: Knowledge Consisting of What Has Been Heard.

1.1.2. Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in Virtue (Sīlamayañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom regarding restraint after having heard [the teaching] is knowledge consisting in virtue? There are five virtues (sīla): [the virtue of abstaining from killing, the virtue of abstaining from taking what is not given, the virtue of abstaining from sexual misconduct, the virtue of abstaining from false speech, and the virtue of abstaining from intoxicants that cause heedlessness.
These are the five virtues.
The virtue of limited purity, the virtue of unlimited purity, the virtue of fulfilled purity, the virtue of unadulterated purity, and the virtue of serenity-purity.
Therein, what is the virtue of limited purity?
It is the limited training precepts for those who are not fully ordained.
This is virtue of limited purity.
What is virtue of unlimited purity? It is the virtue of those who are fully ordained with respect to the training rules that are unlimited.
This is morality of boundless purity.
What is morality of fulfilled purity?
It is that of the virtuous worldlings who are devoted to wholesome states, who fulfill their practice up to the limit of the trainees, and who, regardless of body or life, have renounced their lives.
This is the virtue of fulfilled purity.
What is the virtue of unassailable purity?
It is that of the seven trainees (sekha).
This is virtue purified by non-transgression.
What is virtue purified by tranquillization?
It is the virtue of the Tathāgata’s disciples whose taints are destroyed, of the Paccekabuddhas, and of the Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
This is the virtue of purification through subsiding.
There is virtue that is limited, and there is virtue that is unlimited.
In this regard, what is that virtue which is limited?
There is virtue limited by gain; there is virtue limited by fame; there is virtue limited by relatives; there is virtue limited by limbs;
there is virtue limited by life. What is that virtue limited by gain?
Here, someone, for the sake of gain, with gain as cause, with gain as motive, transgresses a training rule as it has been undertaken.
This is that virtue which has gain as its limit.
What is that virtue which has fame as its limit?
Here, someone, for the sake of fame, with fame as the cause, and with fame as the motive, transgresses a training rule as it was undertaken.
This is virtue limited by fame.
What is that virtue limited by relatives?
Here, someone, for the sake of relatives, on account of relatives, because of relatives, transgresses a training rule as it has been undertaken.
This is that virtue limited by relatives.
What is that virtue limited by limbs?
Here, someone, for the sake of a limb, on account of a limb, because of a limb, transgresses a training rule as it has been undertaken.
This is that virtue which has its limit in the [specific] factors.
What is that virtue which has its limit in life?
Here, someone, for the sake of life, on account of life, and by reason of life, transgresses a training rule as it was undertaken.
This is that virtue which lasts as long as life.
Such virtues as these— broken, flawed, mottled, stained, unliberated, not praised by the wise, adhered to,
not conducive to concentration, not a basis for non-regret, and not a basis for gladness— are [not true virtue].
They do not have rapture as their basis, nor serenity as their basis, nor happiness as their basis, nor concentration as their basis,
nor the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as their basis; they do not lead to utter disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace,
nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.
This is that virtue which has a limit. What is that virtue which is unlimited? There is virtue that does not have gain as its limit;

there is virtue that does not have fame as its limit; there is virtue that does not have relatives as its limit; there is virtue that does not have limbs as its limit; there is virtue that does not have life as its limit.
What is that virtue which does not have gain as its limit?

Here, someone, for the sake of gain, with gain as cause, and with gain as motive, does not even give rise to the thought of transgressing a training rule as it has been undertaken; how much less would he actually transgress it?
This is that virtue which does not have gain as its limit.
What is that virtue which does not have fame as its limit?

Here, someone, for the sake of fame, on account of fame, and because of fame, does not even give rise to a thought of transgressing a training rule as it has been undertaken; how much less would he actually transgress it?
This is that virtue which does not have fame as its limit.
What is that virtue which does not have relatives as its limit?

Here, someone—on account of relatives, conditioned by relatives, for the sake of relatives—does not even give rise to a thought of transgressing a training rule as it has been undertaken; how much less would he actually transgress it?
This is that virtue which does not have relatives as its limit.
What is that virtue which does not have its limit in the factors?

Here, someone—on account of a factor, by reason of a factor, for the sake of a factor—does not even give rise to a thought toward the transgression of a training rule as it has been undertaken; how then would he transgress it?
This is that virtue which does not have its limit in the factors.
What is that virtue which does not have its limit in life?

Here, someone, for the sake of life, on account of life, and for the purpose of life, does not even give rise to a thought of transgressing the training rule as it has been undertaken; how much less would he actually transgress it?
This is that virtue which does not have its limit in life.
Such virtues are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating,
praised by the wise, unadhered-to, conducive to concentration, and serve as the basis for non-regret, the basis for gladness, the basis for rapture,
the basis for tranquility, the basis for happiness, the basis for concentration, and the basis for knowledge and vision of things as they truly are.
They lead to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna—
this is that virtue which is boundless.
What is that virtue?
How many kinds of virtue are there?
What is the origination of virtue?
How many factors constitute virtue?
What is virtue? Volition is virtue, mental factors are virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue.
How many kinds of virtue are there? There are three kinds of virtue:
wholesome virtue, unwholesome virtue, and indeterminate virtue.

What is the origination of virtue? Virtue originated by wholesome consciousness is wholesome virtue; virtue originated by unwholesome consciousness is unwholesome virtue; virtue originated by indeterminate consciousness is indeterminate virtue. In how many ways is virtue the convergence of phenomena?
Virtue is the convergence of restraint; virtue is the convergence of non-transgression; virtue is the convergence of volition born of suchness.
The abstention from taking life is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Taking what is not given is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Sexual misconduct is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
False speech is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Divisive speech is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Harsh speech is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Idle chatter is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Covetousness is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Ill will is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Wrong view is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
Through renunciation, sensual desire is restrained; in the sense of restraint it is virtue, and in the sense of non-transgression it is virtue.
Through non-ill will, ill will is restrained; in the sense of restraint it is virtue, and in the sense of non-transgression it is virtue.
Through the perception of light, sloth and torpor [are restrained]...
Restlessness through the sense of non-distraction;
doubt through the discernment of phenomena;
ignorance through knowledge.
… dispel discontent with joy.
… [dispel] the hindrances with the first jhāna;
… [dispel] applied and sustained thought with the second jhāna.
By means of the third jhāna, [he abandons] rapture;
by means of the fourth jhāna, pleasure and pain;
by means of the attainment of the base of infinite space, the perception of form, the perception of sensory reaction, and the perception of diversity.
the perception of the base of infinite space in the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness;
the perception of the base of infinite consciousness in the attainment of the base of nothingness;
and the perception of the base of nothingness in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Through the contemplation of impermanence, the perception of permanence [is abandoned];
through the contemplation of suffering, the perception of pleasure;
through the contemplation of non-self, the perception of self.
Through the contemplation of disenchantment, [one abandons] delight; through the contemplation of dispassion, [one abandons] lust;
through the contemplation of cessation, [one abandons] origination.
Grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment;
the perception of solidity through the contemplation of destruction;
and accumulation through the contemplation of vanishing.
Through the contemplation of change, the perception of permanence;
through the contemplation of the signless, the sign;
through the contemplation of the desireless, desire.
the adherence to [the notion of] self through the contemplation of emptiness;
the adherence to grasping at a core through higher wisdom and insight into phenomena;
and the adherence to delusion through the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are.
Through the contemplation of danger, one abandons adherence to a basis;
through the contemplation of reflection, one abandons lack of reflection;
through the contemplation of turning away, one abandons adherence to bondage.
By means of the path of stream-entry, the defilements associated with views;
by means of the path of once-returning, the gross defilements;
by means of the path of non-returning, the subtle defilements.
By means of the path of arahantship, virtue is so called in the sense of restraint regarding all defilements; virtue is so called in the sense of non-transgression.
There are five kinds of virtue:
the abandoning of the destruction of life is virtue; abstention is virtue; volition is virtue; restraint is virtue; non-transgression is virtue.
Such virtues lead to non-regret in the mind; they lead to gladness; they lead to rapture;
they lead to tranquility; they lead to joy; they lead to cultivation; they lead to development;
they lead to frequent practice; they lead to adornment; they lead to equipment.
They lead to convergence, they lead to support, they lead to fulfillment; they lead to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
The restraint and purity of such virtues is higher virtue (*adhisīla*); the mind established in that purity of restraint—
It does not fall into distraction; the purity of non-distraction is right view regarding the purity of higher mind and the purity of restraint.
The purity of vision is higher wisdom.
The aspect of restraint therein is the training in higher virtue;
the aspect of non-distraction therein is the training in higher mind;
the aspect of vision therein is the training in higher wisdom.
One trains by reflecting upon these three trainings; one trains knowing them, one trains seeing them,
one trains reviewing them, one trains resolving the mind upon them, one trains being resolved through faith,
one trains exerting energy, one trains establishing mindfulness, one trains concentrating the mind, and [one trains] through wisdom.
One trains while understanding; one trains while directly knowing what is to be directly known; one trains while fully understanding what is to be fully understood;
one trains while abandoning what is to be abandoned; one trains while realizing what is to be realized; one trains while developing what is to be developed. The five precepts:
Of taking what is not given … of sexual misconduct … of false speech …
...of malicious speech ...
of harsh speech ...
of idle chatter ...
Of covetousness … of ill will … of wrong view …
By means of renunciation, [one abandons] sensual desire;
by means of non-ill will, ill will;
by means of the perception of light, sloth and torpor.
Through non-distraction, [one abandons] restlessness;
through the discernment of phenomena, doubt;
through knowledge, ignorance.
By means of gladness, [one abandons] discontent;
by the first jhāna, the hindrances;
by the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought.
By means of the third jhāna, [one is liberated] from rapture;
by means of the fourth jhāna, from pleasure and pain;
by means of the attainment of the base of infinite space, from the perception of form, the perception of sensory impact, and the perception of diversity.
of the perception of the base of infinite space in relation to the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness; ...
of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness in relation to the attainment of the base of nothingness; ...
of the perception of the base of nothingness in relation to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; ...
Through the contemplation of impermanence, [one abandons] the perception of permanence;
through the contemplation of suffering, the perception of pleasure;
through the contemplation of non-self, the perception of self.
Through the contemplation of disenchantment, [one abandons] delight;
through the contemplation of dispassion, [one abandons] lust;
through the contemplation of cessation, [one abandons] origination.
of grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment;
of the perception of solidity through the contemplation of destruction;
and of accumulation through the contemplation of vanishing.
Through the contemplation of change, [one abandons] the perception of permanence;
through the contemplation of the signless, the sign;
through the contemplation of the desireless, desire.
...of the adherence to [the notion of] self through the contemplation of emptiness;
...of the adherence to craving for essence through the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena;
...of the adherence to delusion through the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are.
Through the contemplation of danger, there is the relinquishing of adherence to attachment;
through the contemplation of reflection, there is the relinquishing of non-reflection;
and through the contemplation of turning away, there is the relinquishing of adherence to bondage.
By means of the path of stream-entry, of those defilements associated with views;
by means of the path of once-returning, of coarse defilements;
by means of the path of non-returning, of residual defilements.
The abandoning of all defilements by means of the path of arahantship is virtue; refraining is virtue; volition is virtue; restraint is virtue; non-transgression is virtue.
Such virtues lead to non-regret in the mind; they lead to gladness; they lead to rapture;
they lead to tranquility; they lead to joy; they lead to cultivation.
They lead to development, they lead to frequent practice, they lead to adornment,
they lead to equipment, they lead to retinue, they lead to fulfillment; they lead to utter disenchantment,
dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
The restraint and purity of such virtues is higher virtue (*adhisīla*).
A mind established in the purity of restraint proceeds to non-distraction; this purity of non-distraction is higher consciousness (*adhicitta*).
One correctly sees the purity of restraint; one correctly sees the purity of non-distraction.
Purification by vision is higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
Whatever therein is the sense of restraint (*saṃvara*), that is the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
Whatever therein is the sense of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), that is the training in higher consciousness (*adhicitta-sikkhā*).
Whatever therein is the meaning of seeing, that is the training in higher wisdom.

One trains by being attentive to these three trainings; one trains by knowing, one trains by seeing, one trains by reviewing, one trains by resolving the mind, and one trains by being resolved through faith, [and] energy...
He trains himself by exerting effort; he trains himself by establishing mindfulness; he trains himself by concentrating the mind; he trains himself by understanding with wisdom;
he trains himself by directly knowing what is to be directly known; he trains himself by fully understanding what is to be fully understood;
he trains himself by abandoning what is to be abandoned; he trains himself by realizing what is to be realized; he trains himself by developing what is to be developed.
In the sense of knowing it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom regarding restraint after having heard is knowledge consisting in virtue."
The second chapter: The Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in Virtue. 1.1.3.
The Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in the Development of Concentration How is it that wisdom in restraining oneself and concentrating is knowledge consisting in the development of concentration?
One concentration:
one-pointedness of mind.
Two concentrations:
Mundane concentration and supramundane concentration.
Three kinds of concentration:

concentration with applied thought and sustained thought, concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Four kinds of concentration:
concentration partaking of decline, concentration partaking of stability, concentration partaking of distinction, and concentration partaking of penetration.
Five kinds of concentration:
The pervasion of rapture, the pervasion of happiness, the pervasion of the mind, the pervasion of light, and the sign for reviewing.
Six kinds of concentration:
through the recollection of the Buddha, one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind is concentration; through the recollection of the Dhamma, one-pointedness of the mind... [is concentration].
One-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration: through the recollection of the Sangha, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration;
through the recollection of virtue, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration; through the recollection of generosity, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration;
through the recollection of the deities, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration.
Seven kinds of mastery over concentration: mastery over concentration, mastery over the attainment of concentration, mastery over the maintenance of concentration,
mastery over emergence from concentration, mastery over the pliancy of concentration, mastery over the range of concentration, and mastery over the directing of concentration.
Eight kinds of concentration:
concentration as one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of the earth-kasina; [concentration] by means of the water-kasina … by means of the fire-kasina … [and so on].
By means of the air kasiṇa … by means of the blue kasiṇa … by means of the yellow kasiṇa …
Concentration is the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of the red kasiṇa … the white kasiṇa.
There are nine kinds of concentration:
There is concentration pertaining to the form realm that is inferior, there is that which is middling, and there is that which is superior;
there is concentration pertaining to the formless realm that is inferior, there is that which is middling, and there is that which is superior;
there is empty concentration, signless concentration, and wishless concentration.
Ten kinds of concentration:
concentration as one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of the perception of a bloated corpse; by means of the perception of a livid corpse;
by means of the perception of a festering corpse... [and so on].
by means of the perception of the fissured … by means of the perception of the gnawed … by means of the perception of the scattered …
by way of the perception of the mutilated and scattered,
by way of the perception of the bloody,
and by way of the perception of the worm-infested; ...
One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction by means of the perception of a skeleton is concentration (*samādhi*).
These are the fifty-five kinds of concentration.
Furthermore, there are twenty-five bases of concentration for concentration:
Concentration in the sense of grasping; concentration in the sense of retinue; concentration in the sense of fulfillment; concentration in the sense of one-pointedness;
concentration in the sense of non-distraction; concentration in the sense of non-dispersal; concentration in the sense of being untroubled;
concentration in the sense of imperturbability; concentration in the sense of liberation; concentration because of the mind’s stability through the establishment of unity; [concentration] evenly...

It is called *samādhi* because it seeks what is even (*sama*); it is called *samādhi* because it does not seek what is uneven (*visama*). It is called *samādhi* because of seeking what is even; it is called *samādhi* because of not seeking what is uneven.
It is called *samādhi* because it takes up what is even; it is called *samādhi* because it does not take up what is uneven.

It is called *samādhi* because of having taken up what is even; it is called *samādhi* because of not having taken up what is uneven. It is called *samādhi* because it practices what is even; it is called *samādhi* because it does not practice what is uneven.
Concentration (*samādhi*): it is concentration because one has practiced rightly; it is concentration because one has not practiced wrongly;

it is concentration because one meditates rightly; it is concentration because one consumes what is wrong; it is concentration because of having rightly consumed; it is concentration because of having consumed what is wrong;
and it is concentration because it is even, beneficial, and blissful.
These twenty-five are the foundations of concentration for concentration.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:

“Wisdom in the concentrating after having restrained is knowledge consisting in the development of concentration. This is the third section: the Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in the Development of Concentration.
1.1.4. The Exposition of Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).
How is it that wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena?

Ignorance is the arising-stability, the occurrence-stability, the sign-stability, the accumulation-stability, the fetter-stability, the impediment-stability, the origination-stability, the cause-stability, and the condition-stability of volitional formations.
In these nine ways ignorance is the condition, and volitional formations are the things arisen from that condition.
"Both these phenomena are dependently arisen"—
this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
[This applies] even to the past period...
In the future time as well, ignorance is the standing-point for the arising of formations, the standing-point for their occurrence, the standing-point for their sign,
the standing-point for their accumulation, the standing-point for their bondage, the standing-point for their impediment, the standing-point for their origin, the standing-point for their cause,
and the standing-point for their condition.
In these nine ways, ignorance is the condition and formations are conditionally arisen.
Both these phenomena are conditionally arisen—
this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
Volitional formations [are the condition] for consciousness...
consciousness [is the condition] for name-and-form...
name-and-form [is the condition] for the six sense bases...
The six sense bases are the condition for contact;
contact is the condition for feeling;
feeling is the condition for craving.
Craving is the condition for clinging;
clinging is the condition for existence;
