existence is the condition for birth.
Birth is the arising, the stationing, the occurrence, the sign, the accumulation, the fetter, the impediment, the origin, the cause, and the condition for aging-and-death.
In these nine ways birth is a condition; aging-and-death is conditionally arisen.
Both these phenomena are conditionally arisen—thus one understands.
Wisdom regarding the comprehension of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
In the past period...
and in the future period as well, there is the arising-stability, the occurrence-stability, and the sign-stability of birth, aging, and death.
And there is the state of accumulation, the state of persistence, the state of bondage, the state of obstruction, the state of origination, the state of cause,
and the state of condition.
In these nine ways, birth is the condition, and aging-and-death is what has arisen by way of that condition.
"Both these phenomena are dependently arisen"—this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
Ignorance is the cause; volitional formations are dependently arisen from that cause.
"Both these phenomena are arisen by way of cause"—
this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
[The same applies to] the past time...
In the future time as well, ignorance is the cause and formations are cause-originated.
Both these states are cause-originated—
wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
Volitional formations are the cause; consciousness is causally arisen.
… [and so on] … Consciousness is the cause; name-and-form is causally arisen.
… Name-and-form is the cause; the six sense bases are causally arisen. …
The six sense bases are the cause; contact is arisen from a cause.
Contact is the cause; feeling is arisen from a cause.
Feeling is the cause; craving is arisen from a cause.
Craving is the cause; clinging is cause-born.
Clinging is the cause; existence is cause-born.
Existence is the cause; birth is cause-born.
Birth is a cause; aging-and-death is cause-originated.
Both these phenomena are cause-originated—this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
In the past time...
and in the future time, birth is the cause and aging-and-death are cause-arisen.
Both these phenomena are cause-arisen—thus it is said.
Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
Dependent on ignorance, volitional formations arise dependently;
both these phenomena are dependently arisen—thus [one understands].
Wisdom regarding the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
In the past time...
and in the future time as well, conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations have arisen dependently.
"Both these states are dependently arisen"—this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
Formations are dependent; consciousness is dependently arisen... [and so on].
Dependent upon consciousness, name-and-form is dependently arisen;
dependent upon name-and-form, the six sense bases are dependently arisen;
dependent upon the six sense bases, contact is dependently arisen.
Contact is dependent; feeling is dependently arisen.
… Feeling is dependent; craving is dependently arisen.
… Craving is dependent; clinging is dependently arisen.
Dependent upon clinging, becoming is dependently arisen; ...
becoming is dependent, birth is dependently arisen; ...
birth is dependent, aging-and-death is dependently arisen.
"These two states are dependently arisen"—
this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
[The same applies] to the past time...
In the future period as well, birth is dependent, and aging-and-death is dependently arisen.
Both these phenomena are dependently arisen—
wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
Ignorance is the condition; volitional formations are conditionally arisen.
Understanding that both these phenomena are conditionally arisen is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena in the discernment of conditions.
In the past time...
and in the future time, ignorance is the condition and formations are conditionally arisen.
Both these phenomena are conditionally arisen—thus [it is said].
Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
Formations are the condition; consciousness is what has arisen through that condition.
… [and so on] … Consciousness is the condition; name-and-form is what has arisen through that condition.
Name-and-form is the condition; the six sense bases are the dependently arisen.
… The six sense bases are the condition; contact is the dependently arisen.
… Contact is the condition; feeling is the dependently arisen.
Feeling is a condition; craving is conditionally arisen.
… Craving is a condition; clinging is conditionally arisen.
… Clinging is a condition; existence is conditionally arisen.
Existence is a condition; birth is what has arisen through that condition.
… Birth is a condition; aging-and-death is what has arisen through that condition.
Both these phenomena have arisen through conditions.
Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
In the past time...
and in the future time as well, birth is the condition, and aging-and-death is what has arisen through that condition.
"Both these phenomena are dependently arisen"—
this wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).

In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance (*avijjā*), the exertion is volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), the attachment is craving (*taṇhā*), the approaching is clinging (*upādāna*), and the intention is becoming (*bhava*).
These five things, in a previous state of existence (purimakammabhava), are conditions for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) here.
Here, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent [into the womb] is name-and-form; the sensitivity is the sense base; the touched is contact; and what is felt is feeling.
These five things, in this state of rebirth (upapattibhava), are conditions for the karma performed previously.
Here, due to the ripening of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance; accumulation is volitional formations; attachment is craving; approaching is clinging; and intention is existence.
These five factors are the conditions here for the kamma-existence to lead to rebirth-linking in the future.
In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent [into the womb] is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense base; what is touched is contact; and what is felt is feeling.
These five factors are the conditions for the future existence-rebirth of the karma performed here [in this life].
Thus, one knows, sees, understands, and penetrates dependent origination—comprising four groups, three time periods, and twenty modes—in these twenty ways.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*); in the sense of full understanding, it is wisdom (*paññā*).
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
This is the fourth exposition: Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena.
1.1.5. Exposition of the Knowledge of Comprehension How is it that wisdom in defining past, future, and present phenomena by way of synthesis is knowledge of comprehension?
Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle—[this is the synthesis].
Whether inferior or superior, far or near—all form he defines as impermanent:

this is one mode of comprehension; he defines it as suffering: this is one mode of comprehension; he defines it as non-self: this is one mode of comprehension. Whatever feeling there may be ... [and so on] ... [he defines it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self]. This is one mode of comprehension.
Whatever perception there may be...
whatever formations there may be...
whatever consciousness there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle.

Whether inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness he defines as impermanent: this is one mode of comprehension; he defines it as suffering: this is one mode of comprehension; he defines it as non-self: this is one mode of comprehension. The eye … [and so on] … The final answer to the problem of suffering, according to the Buddha, is the attainment of nibbāna, which is the cessation of all conditioned phenomena. This state is described as the "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata), the "peaceful" (santa), and the "noble" (ariya). It is not a place to be reached, nor a thing to be acquired, but rather a transformation of consciousness that occurs when the mind is completely free from the three root defilements: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). Nibbāna is often characterized by the absence of these defilements. It is the "blowing out" of the fires of passion, aversion, and ignorance. In its ultimate sense, it is the end of the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth (saṃsāra). While it is ineffable and beyond conceptualization, it can be pointed to through the cessation of the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) at the moment of enlightenment. For the practitioner who has realized it, it is experienced as supreme peace and liberation. Those who have attained it are called "arahants," for they have "gone forth" from the world of becoming and will never again be subject to future suffering. Thus, the path to the cessation of suffering leads directly to the realization of this unconditioned state, where all mental formations (saṅkhārā) have come to rest.

One discerns aging-and-death—past, future, and present—as impermanent: this is one comprehension. One discerns it as suffering: this is one comprehension. One discerns it as non-self: this is one comprehension.

Wisdom in defining form—past, future, and present—by way of its summary as "impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness," is knowledge of comprehension.
[The same applies to] feeling …pe… [and so on].
Perception … [and so on] … volitional formations … [and so on] … consciousness … [and so on].

Wisdom in defining, by way of summary, that the eye— and so on up to— aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness,

is knowledge of comprehension. Wisdom in defining, by way of summary, that form— whether past, future, or present— is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, is knowledge of comprehension.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …

The wisdom in defining, by way of summarizing, that consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, is knowledge of comprehension.
"Conditioned by birth is aging-and-death; in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death"—wisdom in defining this by way of summary is knowledge of comprehension.
"In the past period...
in the future period, conditioned by birth is aging-and-death; in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death"—wisdom in defining this by way of summary is knowledge of comprehension.
With existence as condition, birth [occurs]; when there is no [existence], ... pe ...
with clinging as condition, existence [occurs]; when there is no [clinging], ... pe ...
with craving as condition, clinging [occurs]; when there is no [craving], ... pe ...
With feeling as condition, craving arises; when [feeling] is absent... pe ...
with contact as condition, feeling arises; when [contact] is absent... pe ...
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; when [the six sense bases] are absent... pe ...
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise]; when there is no [name-and-form]... [as before] ...
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]; when there is no [consciousness]... [as before] ...
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness [arises]; when there is no [volitional formations]... [as before] ...
"Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; in the absence of ignorance, there are no volitional formations"—wisdom in defining this by way of summary is knowledge of comprehension.
"In the past period...

and in the future period, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; in the absence of ignorance, there are no volitional formations"—wisdom in defining this by way of summary is knowledge of comprehension.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom in the defining of past, future, and present phenomena by way of synthesis is knowledge in comprehension."
The Fifth Exposition: Knowledge of Comprehension (Sammasanañāṇaniddesa). 1.1.6.

Exposition of Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbayañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom in contemplating the change of presently arisen phenomena is knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away?
Material form that has arisen is present; its characteristic of production is arising, its characteristic of transformation is passing away, and the knowledge that contemplates this is wisdom.
Feeling that has arisen… perception that has arisen…
Formations are born;
consciousness is born;
the eye is born... [and so on] ...up to... [the mind and mental phenomena].
Existence that has arisen is present; its characteristic of production is arising (*udaya*), its characteristic of transformation is passing away (*vaya*), and the contemplation thereof is knowledge.

When one contemplates the arising of the five aggregates, how many characteristics does one see? When contemplating their passing away, how many characteristics does one see? When contemplating both their arising and passing away, how many characteristics does one see?
Contemplating the arising of the five aggregates, one sees twenty-five characteristics; contemplating their passing away, one sees twenty-five characteristics.
One who sees arising and passing away sees fifty characteristics.

When seeing the arising of the aggregate of form, how many characteristics does one see? When seeing its passing away, how many characteristics does one see? When seeing both its arising and passing away, how many characteristics does one see?
[The same applies to] the aggregate of feeling... [and so on].

When one sees the arising of the aggregate of perception …pe… the aggregate of volitional formations …pe… the aggregate of consciousness, how many characteristics does one see? When one sees its passing away, how many characteristics does one see? When one sees both its arising and its passing away, how many characteristics does one see?
One who sees the arising of the aggregate of form sees five characteristics; one who sees its passing away sees five characteristics;

“Arising is formations”; he looks on with equanimity at those formations—this is [knowledge of equanimity regarding formations].
Equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

Both those formations and that equanimity—all these are formations; one looks on with equanimity at those formations—thus it is "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
In how many ways does the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations occur?
The mind’s directing of itself toward equanimity regarding formations occurs in eight ways.
In how many ways does the mind’s directing of itself toward equanimity regarding formations occur for an ordinary person?
In how many ways does the mind’s directing of itself toward equanimity regarding formations occur for one in training?
In how many ways does the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations occur for one who is free from lust?
For an ordinary person, the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations occurs in two ways.
For one in training, the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations occurs in three ways.
For one who is free from lust, there is a directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations in three ways.
For an ordinary person, in which two ways is there a directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations?
An ordinary person either delights in equanimity regarding formations or contemplates them with insight.
For an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) occurs in these two ways.
For one in training (*sekkha*), in what three ways does the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations occur?

One in training either delights in equanimity regarding formations, or practices insight (*vipassati*), or, through reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāya*), enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
In these three ways, there is a directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations for one in training (*sekkha*).
For one free from lust (*vītarāga*), in what three ways is there a directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations?

One free from lust either contemplates with insight (*vipassati*) or, having reflected, enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); or, having looked upon that with equanimity, he dwells in the dwelling of emptiness, the signless dwelling, or the desireless dwelling.
For one who is free from lust, the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations occurs through these three modes.
How is it that the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations is the same for both the worldling and the trainee?
When a worldling delights in equanimity regarding formations, his mind becomes defiled; it becomes an obstacle to development, an impediment to penetration, and a condition for future rebirth.

Even for a trainee (*sekkha*), if he delights in equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), his mind becomes defiled; it becomes an obstacle to development, an impediment to further penetration, and a condition for future rebirth.
Thus, for both the worldling (*puthujjana*) and the trainee, the directing of the mind toward equanimity toward formations is the same in the sense of delighting in it.
How is it that for the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust (*vītarāga*), the directing of the mind toward equanimity toward formations is the same?
The worldling contemplates equanimity toward formations as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self.
The trainee also contemplates equanimity toward formations as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self.
One who is free from lust also contemplates equanimity toward formations as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self.
Thus, for the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust, the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations is a unity in the sense of contemplation.
How is it that for the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust, the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations is a diversity?
For the worldling, equanimity regarding formations is wholesome.
For one in training (*sekkha*), equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) is wholesome (*kusala*).
For one free from lust (*vītarāga*), equanimity toward formations is indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Thus, there is a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity toward formations for the worldling, the one in training, and the one free from lust, in terms of being wholesome or indeterminate.

In what way is there a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), one in training (*sekkha*), and one who is free from lust (*vītarāga*)?
For an ordinary person, equanimity regarding formations is well understood at some times and not well understood at other times.
For one in training as well, equanimity regarding formations is well understood at some times and not well understood at other times.
For one who is free from lust, equanimity regarding formations is thoroughly well-known.

Thus, there is a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations for the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust, by way of what is known and what is not yet known.
How is there a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations for the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust?
The worldling contemplates equanimity toward formations because he is not yet satisfied with it.
The trainee also contemplates equanimity toward formations because he is not yet satisfied with it.
One who is free from lust contemplates equanimity toward formations because he is satisfied with it.

Thus, there is a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations among the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust, by way of being satisfied and unsatisfied.
How is there a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations among the worldling, the trainee, and the one free from lust?
The worldling contemplates equanimity regarding formations with insight for the sake of abandoning the three fetters and for the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry.
The trainee contemplates equanimity towards formations for the sake of attaining what is higher, because of having abandoned three fetters.
One free from lust contemplates equanimity towards formations for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, because of having abandoned all defilements.

Thus there is a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity towards formations among the worldling, the trainee, and one free from lust, by way of what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned.
How is there a difference in the mental application of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) for one who is still in training (*sekkha*) and for one who is free from lust (*vītarāga*)?

The one in training either delights in equanimity toward formations, or contemplates them with insight (*vipassati*), or, having reflected upon them, enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

The one free from lust either contemplates equanimity toward formations or, having reflected upon them, enters the attainment of fruition; but having looked upon that with equanimity, he dwells in the dwelling of emptiness (*suññatavihāra*), the dwelling of the signless (*animittavihāra*), or the dwelling of the desireless (*appaṇihitavihāra*).
Thus, there is a difference in the directing of the mind toward equanimity regarding formations for one in training and for one free from lust, in terms of their respective dwellings and attainments.

How many types of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight?
Eight equanimities regarding formations arise by way of serenity;

Which eight equanimities regarding formations arise by way of serenity?
Wisdom that consists in reflective composure regarding the hindrances for the sake of attaining the first jhāna is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
Wisdom that consists in reflective composure regarding applied thought and sustained thought for the sake of attaining the second jhāna is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
Wisdom that consists in reflective composure regarding rapture for the sake of attaining the third jhāna is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
Wisdom that reflects upon and remains equanimous toward pleasure and pain for the sake of attaining the fourth jhāna is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations.

Wisdom that reflects upon and remains equanimous toward the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of infinite space is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations.

Wisdom that reflects upon and remains equanimous toward the perception of the base of infinite space for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations.

Wisdom that reflects upon and settles the perception of the base of infinite consciousness for the purpose of attaining the attainment of the base of nothingness is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.

Wisdom that reflects upon and settles the perception of the base of nothingness for the purpose of attaining the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
These eight kinds of equanimity towards formations arise by way of serenity.
What are the ten kinds of equanimity towards formations that arise by way of insight?
They are the equanimity of reflective stability regarding arising, occurrence, sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking,
destiny, generation, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and despair, for the purpose of attaining the path of stream-entry.

Exposition of Path-Knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa) How is it that wisdom regarding the emergence from both sides and the turning away [from defilements] is knowledge of the path?

At the moment of the path of stream-entry, right view in the sense of seeing emerges from wrong view; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the emergence and turning away from both sides is knowledge of the path."
In the sense of directing, right intention emerges from wrong intention; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom in the turning away and emerging from both sides is knowledge of the path.”
In the sense of embracing, right speech emerges from wrong speech; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path.”
In the sense of its origination, right action emerges from wrong action; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon it, and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path.”
In the sense of cleansing, right livelihood emerges from wrong livelihood; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path.”
In the sense of exertion, right effort emerges from wrong effort; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path.”

In the sense of being established, right mindfulness emerges from wrong mindfulness; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path."

Right concentration, in the sense of non-distraction, emerges from wrong concentration; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path."

"The wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path."

"He does not waver amidst various views":
in the sense of knowing, it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*); in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom (*paññā*).

“Wisdom regarding emergence and turning away from both sides is knowledge of the path.
This concludes the eleventh exposition: the Exposition of Knowledge of the Path.
1.1.12. Exposition of Knowledge of the Fruit.
How is it that the wisdom of the subsiding of the preliminary task is knowledge of the fruit?

At the moment of the stream-entry path, right view—in the sense of seeing—emerges from wrong view; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon it, and it emerges from all external signs.
Because that preliminary task has subsided, right view arises.
This is the fruit of the path.
In the sense of directing, right intention emerges from wrong intention; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Right intention arises because the application [to those things] has subsided.
This is the fruit of the path.
In the sense of embracing, right speech emerges from wrong speech; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon it, and it emerges from all external signs.
Right speech arises because of the subsiding of the application thereto.
This is the fruit of the Path.
In the sense of emergence, right action emerges from wrong action; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Right action arises because the application [to those things] has subsided.
This is the fruit of the path.
In the sense of purification, right livelihood emerges from wrong livelihood; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon it, and it emerges from all external signs.
Right livelihood arises because the application [to those things] has been stilled.
This is the fruit of the path.
In the sense of exertion, right effort emerges from wrong effort; it emerges from the defilements and the aggregates that follow upon it, and it emerges from all external signs.
Right effort arises because of the subsiding of the application [to those things].
This is the fruit of the path.
In the sense of establishing, right mindfulness emerges from wrong mindfulness; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Right mindfulness arises because of the subsiding of the application [to those things].
This is the fruit of the path.

In the sense of non-distraction, right concentration emerges from wrong concentration; it emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.
Right concentration arises because the application for those [defilements] has been stilled.
This is the fruit of the path.
At the moment of the once-returning path: right view in the sense of seeing … [and so on] … right concentration in the sense of non-distraction;
the gross fetters of sensual lust and ill will, and the gross underlying tendencies of sensual lust … [and so on] … are abandoned.
One emerges from the underlying tendency to aversion; one emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates;
and one emerges from all external signs.
Through the subsiding of that application, right concentration arises.
This is the fruit of the path.
At the moment of the non-returning path, right view in the sense of seeing ... pe ...
right concentration in the sense of non-distraction is associated with the fetters of sensual lust and ill will that are not yet abandoned.
One emerges from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion; one emerges from the defilements that follow upon them and from the aggregates;
and one emerges from all external signs.
Through the subsiding of that application, right concentration arises.
This is the fruit of the path.
At the moment of the path of arahantship, right view in the sense of seeing … [and so on] … right concentration in the sense of non-distraction;
[the abandoning of] lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, and the underlying tendency to conceit.
One emerges from the underlying tendency to lust for existence and the underlying tendency to ignorance; one emerges from the defilements that follow upon them and from the aggregates;
and one emerges from all external signs.
Through the subsiding of the application toward those [signs], right concentration arises.
This is the fruit of the path.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is called:
“Wisdom as the subsiding of the application [of the path] is knowledge of the fruit.
This concludes the twelfth exposition: Knowledge of the Fruit. 1.1.13.
Exposition of Knowledge of Liberation.
How is it that wisdom in contemplating the cutting off of the stream is knowledge of liberation?

By means of the path of stream-entry, personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, the underlying tendency to personality-belief, and the underlying tendency to doubt—these defilements of one’s own mind—are completely cut off.
With the mind liberated from these five defilements along with their obsessions, it is well-liberated.
That liberation is knowledge in the sense of having been known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the contemplation of the path as cut off is the knowledge of liberation."

By means of the path of once-returning, the gross fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to aversion—these defilements of one’s own mind—are completely cut off.
The mind is liberated from these four defilements along with their obsessions; it is well-liberated.
That liberation is knowledge in the sense of having been known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the contemplation of the path that has been cut off is the knowledge of liberation."

By means of the path of non-returning, the fetter of sensual lust accompanied by underlying tendency, the fetter of ill will, the underlying tendency to sensual lust accompanied by underlying tendency, and the underlying tendency to ill will—these defilements of one’s own mind are completely severed.
The mind is liberated from these four defilements along with their obsessions; it is well-liberated.
That liberation is knowledge in the sense of having known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the contemplation of the path as cut off is the knowledge of liberation."

By means of the path of arahantship, lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance—these defilements of one’s own mind are completely cut off.
The mind is liberated from these eight defilements along with their obsessions; it is well-liberated.
That liberation is knowledge in the sense of having known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the contemplation of the path cut off is the knowledge of liberation."
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in contemplating the cutting off of the path is the knowledge of liberation."

1.1.15. The Description of Knowledge of the Diversity of Bases.
How is it that wisdom in defining the internal is knowledge of the diversity of bases?
How does one define internal phenomena?

One defines the eye as internal; one defines the ear as internal; one defines the nose as internal; one defines the tongue as internal; one defines the body as internal; one defines the mind as internal.
How does one define the eye as internal?
One defines: "The eye is born of ignorance"; one defines: "The eye is born of craving"; one defines: "The eye is born of kamma";
one defines: "The eye is born of nutriment"; one defines: "The eye is derived from the four great elements";
one defines: "The eye has arisen"; one defines: "The eye has come to be."
He defines: "The eye, having not been, has come to be; having been, it will not be.
He defines the eye as finite; he defines the eye as unstable, non-eternal, subject to change.
He defines the eye as impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away.
One defines it as subject to cessation.
One defines the eye as impermanent, not as permanent;
one defines it as suffering, not as pleasure.
One discerns it as non-self, not as self;
one becomes disenchanted with it, not delighted by it;
one becomes dispassionate toward it, not attached to it.
He causes cessation, not arising;
he relinquishes, he does not grasp.
Distinguishing [phenomena] as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence; distinguishing them as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure.
Distinguishing it as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted with it, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate toward it, one abandons lust;
causing its cessation, one abandons origination; relinquishing it, one abandons grasping.
In this way, one defines the eye internally.
How does one define the ear internally?
One defines the ear as arisen from ignorance … [and so on] … In this way one defines the ear internally.
How does one define the nose internally?
One defines the nose as arisen from ignorance … [and so on] … In this way, one defines the nose internally.
How does one define the internal tongue? One defines it thus:

"The tongue is produced from nutriment," one defines it thus: "The tongue is derived from the four great elements."
He defines it: he defines that "the tongue has arisen," he defines that "the tongue has come into being.

he relinquishes it, he does not grasp at it.

one defines it thus: "The body is produced from nutriment"; one defines it thus: "The body is derived from the four great elements."

1.1.17. Exposition of Knowledge of the Diversity of Temperaments.
How is it that wisdom in the discernment of temperaments is knowledge of the diversity of temperaments?
"Conduct" refers to three types of conduct:
the conduct of consciousness, the conduct of ignorance, and the conduct of knowledge.
What is the conduct of consciousness?

The functional-ineffective adverting consciousness is a movement of consciousness regarding forms for the purpose of seeing; eye-consciousness is a movement of consciousness regarding forms in the sense of seeing;
the resultant mind-element is a movement of consciousness regarding forms in the sense of determining what has been seen;
and the resultant mind-consciousness-element is a movement of consciousness regarding forms in the sense of having determined what has been seen.

The functional indeterminate process of adverting for the purpose of hearing is a movement of consciousness regarding sounds; the ear-consciousness, which has the purpose of hearing, is a movement of consciousness regarding sounds;
the resultant mind-element, which performs the function of determining because of what was heard, is a movement of consciousness regarding sounds;
and the resultant mind-consciousness-element, which performs the function of having determined, is a movement of consciousness regarding sounds.

The functional indeterminate advertence for the purpose of smelling is a movement of consciousness regarding odors; the act of smelling, which is nose-consciousness, is a movement of consciousness regarding odors;
the resultant mind-element, which is the determination following what has been smelled, is a movement of consciousness regarding odors;
and the resultant mind-consciousness-element, which follows the determination, is a movement of consciousness regarding odors.

The functional indeterminate advertence for the purpose of tasting is a movement of consciousness regarding tastes; tongue-consciousness is a movement of consciousness regarding tastes in the sense of tasting;
the resultant mind-element is a movement of consciousness regarding tastes in the sense of determining what has been tasted;
and the resultant mind-consciousness-element is a movement of consciousness regarding tastes in the sense of having determined what has been tasted.

The functional-ineffective advertence for the purpose of touching is a movement of consciousness regarding tangibles; body-consciousness, which is the act of touching, is a movement of consciousness regarding tangibles;
the resultant mind-element, which is the application [of attention] due to having been touched, is a movement of consciousness regarding tangibles;
and the resultant mind-consciousness-element, which is the state of having been applied, is a movement of consciousness regarding tangibles.

The course of consciousness consisting of the functional indeterminate adverting [consciousness] for the purpose of impelling lust toward agreeable forms is the course of ignorance;

The functional indeterminate consciousness that acts as the adverting for the purpose of impulsion by doubt—which has reached an undesirable state—is a course of consciousness;
the impulsions of doubt are a course of ignorance.
The cognitive process of functional-ineffective advertence is for the purpose of impelling the latent tendency that has reached a state of stability;
the impulsion of the latent tendency is a cognitive process of ignorance.
[This applies] to agreeable sounds... and so forth.
In regard to pleasing odors … [and so on] … in regard to pleasing tastes … [and so on] … in regard to pleasing tangibles … [and so on] …
The functional-ineffective consciousness-process of adverting for the purpose of impelling lust toward agreeable phenomena is a movement of consciousness;
the impulsion of lust is a movement of ignorance.

The functional-ineffective consciousness-process of adverting for the purpose of impelling hatred toward disagreeable phenomena is a movement of consciousness; [the impulsion of hatred is a movement of ignorance].
The impulsions of hatred are a course of ignorance.

When there is no regard for the object due to both [greed and hatred], the functional indeterminate consciousness that serves as the adverting for the impulsion of delusion is a course of consciousness;
the impulsions of delusion are a course of ignorance.
The functional-ineffective consciousness-process of adverting for the sake of the impulsion of conceit bound by fetters is a course of ignorance;
the impulsion of conceit is a course of ignorance.
The functional-ineffective consciousness-process of adverting for the sake of the impulsion of a view that has been misapprehended is a course of ignorance.
The impulsions of views are a course of ignorance.
For one who has fallen into distraction, the functional indeterminate adverting consciousness is a course of consciousness for the sake of the impulsion of restlessness;
the impulsions of restlessness are a course of ignorance.

The course of consciousness consisting of the functional-ineffective (kiriyā-byākatā) adverting [consciousness] for the purpose of impulsion regarding doubt that has not yet reached its conclusion is the course of ignorance;
the impulsion of doubt is the course of ignorance.

The course of consciousness consisting of the functional-ineffective adverting [consciousness] for the purpose of impulsion regarding an underlying tendency (anusaya) that has become firmly established is [likewise] the course of ignorance.
The impulsions of underlying tendency are the conduct of ignorance.
In what sense is it "the conduct of ignorance"? It is because one conducts oneself with lust—that is why it is called the conduct of ignorance.
The conduct of ignorance.
One conducts oneself with hatred—
this is the conduct of ignorance.
"He acts with delusion" refers to the conduct of ignorance.
"He acts with pride" refers to—
The conduct of ignorance.
It conducts itself with wrong view;
thus it is the conduct of ignorance.
"He conducts himself with agitation"—
this is a way of conduct characterized by ignorance. "He conducts himself with doubt"— this is...
The conduct of ignorance.
It conducts itself with underlying tendencies—
thus it is the conduct of ignorance.
"He conducts himself associated with lust"—
this is the conduct of ignorance. "He conducts himself associated with hatred"— this is the conduct of ignorance.
The conduct of ignorance:
it conducts itself associated with delusion,
thus it is the conduct of ignorance.
"He conducts himself associated with ignorance"—
this is the conduct of ignorance.
"He conducts himself associated with views"— this is...
The course of ignorance.
It courses associated with restlessness—
this is the course of ignorance.
"He courses associated with doubt"—
this is the course of ignorance.
"He courses associated with underlying tendencies"— this is...
The conduct of ignorance.
It conducts itself dissociated from wholesome kamma—
this is the conduct of ignorance.
One who acts associated with unwholesome deeds is said to have a course of ignorance.
One who acts associated with blameworthy deeds is said to have...
The conduct of ignorance.
One conducts oneself dissociated from blameless deeds—
this is the conduct of ignorance.
"One who acts associated with dark deeds" refers to the conduct of ignorance.
"One who acts dissociated from bright deeds" refers to... [the conduct of ignorance].
The conduct of ignorance.
It conducts itself dissociated from actions that have a happy result—
this is the conduct of ignorance.
To practice associated with kamma that has suffering as its outcome is the conduct of ignorance.
To practice dissociated from kamma that has happiness as its ripening is—
The conduct of ignorance:
it conducts itself associated with kamma that has a painful result—
thus it is the conduct of ignorance.
"He conducts himself without knowing" means conduct of ignorance;
such is the kind of conduct belonging to ignorance.
The conduct of ignorance.
This is the conduct of ignorance.
What is the conduct of knowledge?
The functional-ineffective consciousness-process for the purpose of adverting toward the contemplation of impermanence is a consciousness-process;
the contemplation of impermanence is a knowledge-process.
The functional-ineffective consciousness-process for the purpose of adverting toward the contemplation of suffering is a consciousness-process.
Contemplation of suffering is the course of knowledge.
The functional indeterminate act of adverting for the purpose of contemplating non-self is the course of consciousness;
contemplation of non-self is the course of knowledge.
For the purpose of contemplating disenchantment … [and so on] … for the purpose of contemplating fading away … for the purpose of contemplating cessation …
for the purpose of contemplating relinquishment … for the purpose of contemplating destruction … for the purpose of contemplating vanishing …
for the purpose of contemplating change,
for the purpose of contemplating the signless,
and for the purpose of contemplating the desireless...
for the purpose of contemplating emptiness … for the purpose of the higher wisdom that contemplates phenomena … for the purpose of knowledge and vision according to reality …

The cognitive process of consciousness consisting of the functional indeterminate advertence for the purpose of contemplating danger ... and for the purpose of contemplating with reflection is the cognitive process of knowledge,
which is the contemplation with reflection.
The practice of knowledge is the contemplation of turning away.
The path of stream-entry is the practice of knowledge.
The attainment of the fruit of stream-entry is the practice of knowledge.
The path of once-returning is the range of knowledge.
The attainment of the fruit of once-returning is the range of knowledge.
The path of non-returning is the range of knowledge.
The attainment of the fruit of non-returning is a course of knowledge.
The path of arahantship is a course of knowledge.
The attainment of the fruit of arahantship is a course of knowledge.
Regarding "the course of knowledge" (ñāṇacariyā): in what sense is it the "course of knowledge"?
It is the "course of knowledge" because one courses free from passion (nīrāga).
"He dwells free from sloth" refers to the course of knowledge... [and so on] ...
"he does not dwell with underlying tendencies."
The course of knowledge.
It courses dissociated from lust—
thus it is the course of knowledge.
"He conducts himself dissociated from hatred"—this is the conduct of knowledge.
"He conducts himself dissociated from delusion"—this is... [the conduct of knowledge].
The conduct of knowledge.
Dissociated from conceit …pe… dissociated from views …
... dissociated from restlessness ...
dissociated from doubt ...
dissociated from underlying tendencies ...
Associated with wholesome kamma;
dissociated from unwholesome kamma;
dissociated from blameworthy kamma.
Associated with blameless actions;
dissociated from dark actions;
associated with bright actions.
One practices associated with actions that have happiness as their outcome,
dissociated from actions that have suffering as their outcome,
and associated with actions that have a happy result.
The course of knowledge.
It courses dissociated from kamma that has painful fruition—
thus it is the course of knowledge.
"It moves within what is known" is the movement of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*).
Such is the movement of knowledge.
The course of knowledge.
This is the course of knowledge.
The course of consciousness is one thing, the course of ignorance is another, and the course of knowledge is yet another.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the determination of conduct is knowledge of the diversity of conduct."
The seventeenth exposition: Knowledge of the Diversity of Conduct.
1.1.18. Exposition of Knowledge of the Diversity of Planes.
How is it that wisdom in the discernment of four things is knowledge of the diversity of planes?
There are four planes:
the sense-sphere plane, the fine-material sphere plane, the immaterial-sphere plane, and the unincluded plane.
What is the sense-sphere plane?
Taking the Avīci hell as its lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas above,
whatever is within this interval— comprised therein and contained therein— the aggregates, elements, and bases: form, feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness.
This is the sense-sphere plane.
What is the fine-material sphere plane?
Taking the Brahma-world as its lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha devas at its upper limit, whatever [exists] within this—

Those states belonging to this sphere, included within this sphere— the mental and mental concomitant phenomena of one who has attained [meditative absorption], or of one who has been reborn there, or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life—
this is the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-bhūmi).
What is the formless-sphere plane?
Taking as its lower limit the gods who have reached the base of infinite space, and taking as its upper limit the gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
that which lies within this interval— belonging to this sphere and included therein for one who has attained [meditative absorption]— is the formless-sphere plane.
The states of mind and mental factors of one who has been reborn [in the formless realm] or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life—
this is the formless-sphere plane (arūpāvacara-bhūmi).
What is the non-included plane (apariyāpanna-bhūmi)?
The paths that are not included [within the realms], the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—
this is the plane that is not included.
These are the four planes.
Furthermore, there are four other grounds: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of spiritual power,
the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four analytical knowledges, the four modes of practice,
the four objects of focus, the four noble lineages, and the four means of social integration.
The four wheels and the four foundations of Dhamma—these are the four stages.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom in the discernment of four things is knowledge of the diversity of planes.
This is the eighteenth exposition: the description of knowledge of the diversity of planes.

1.1.19. Exposition of the Knowledge of the Diversity of Phenomena (Dhammanānattañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom in the discernment of nine phenomena is knowledge of the diversity of phenomena? How does one discern phenomena?
He defines states belonging to the sense sphere as wholesome, he defines them as unwholesome, and he defines them as indeterminate.
He defines states belonging to the fine-material sphere as wholesome and he defines them as indeterminate.
He defines states belonging to the immaterial sphere as wholesome and he defines them as indeterminate.
He defines states that are not included [within the mundane] as wholesome; he defines them as indeterminate.
How does he define states belonging to the sense sphere as wholesome, as unwholesome, or as indeterminate?
He defines the ten courses of wholesome action as wholesome; he defines the ten courses of unwholesome action as unwholesome; and he defines matter, result, and functional [states] as indeterminate.
In this way, one defines states belonging to the sense sphere as wholesome, defines them as unwholesome, and defines them as indeterminate.
How does one define states belonging to the fine-material sphere as wholesome and as indeterminate?
Here, one defines the four jhānas of one established here [in the human world] as wholesome; one defines the four jhānas of one reborn there [in the fine-material realm] as indeterminate.
In this way, one defines the fine-material-sphere phenomena as wholesome and defines them as indeterminate.
How does one define the immaterial-sphere phenomena as wholesome and define them as indeterminate?

Here, one defines the four immaterial-sphere attainments of one established here [in the sense-sphere] as wholesome; one defines the four immaterial-sphere attainments of one reborn there [in the immaterial realm] as indeterminate.
In this way, one defines the phenomena of the formless realm as wholesome and defines them as indeterminate.
How does one define the phenomena that are not included [within the realms] as wholesome and define them as indeterminate?
One defines the four noble paths as wholesome, and one defines the four fruits of recluseship and Nibbāna as indeterminate.
Thus he defines states that are not included [within the mundane] as wholesome, and he defines them as indeterminate.
In this way he defines states.
These are the nine states rooted in gladness.

When one attends to [the body] as impermanent, gladness arises; in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
With the mind concentrated, one knows and sees things as they truly are.
Knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted; through disenchantment, passion fades away; through the fading of passion, one is liberated.
When one attends to [the body] as suffering,
gladness arises …pe… when one attends to it as non-self,
gladness arises …pe… when one attends to form as impermanent, gladness arises …pe…
For one who attends to form as suffering … pe … [and likewise] to feeling … perception … [and so forth].

Volitional formations … consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … pe … [as before] … the mind … mental phenomena … the mind-consciousness element … the mind-contact element … the feeling arisen from mind-contact … the perception of mind-contact … the volition regarding mind-contact … the attention directed toward mind-contact … the craving for mind-contact … the thought regarding mind-contact … When one attends to aging and death as impermanent, gladness arises … pe … when one attends to aging and death as suffering, gladness arises … pe … when one attends to aging and death as non-self, gladness arises.

For one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
With a concentrated mind, one understands and sees things as they truly are.
Understanding and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated.
These are the nine qualities rooted in gladness.
Nine things rooted in wise attention. For one who attends wisely to impermanence, gladness arises;
in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; for one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated.
With a concentrated mind, one understands as it really is: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering."

One understands it as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering," one understands it as it really is; "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," one understands it as it really is.

When one attends wisely to [suffering] as suffering, gladness arises; for one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
With a concentrated mind, one understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; one understands as it really is:

"This is the origin of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In one who attends wisely to [the self] as non-self,
gladness arises … [as above] … In one who attends wisely to form as impermanent,
gladness arises … [as above] … In one who attends wisely to form as suffering, gladness arises … [as above] …
For one who attends wisely to form as non-self, gladness arises; ... [and so on] ...
to feeling ...
to perception ...
Volitional formations … consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … pe … [as above] …
When one attends wisely to aging and death as impermanent, gladness arises;
... pe ... when one attends wisely to aging and death as suffering, gladness arises;

... pe ... when one attends wisely to aging and death as non-self, gladness arises. For one who is glad, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
With a concentrated mind, one understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; one understands as it really is:

"This is the origin of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
These are the nine things rooted in wise attention.
There are nine diversities:
dependent on the diversity of elements, there arises the diversity of contact; dependent on the diversity of contact, there arises...
The diversity of feelings; dependent on the diversity of feelings, there arises the diversity of perceptions;
dependent on the diversity of perceptions, there arises the diversity of intentions; dependent on the diversity of intentions, there arises the diversity of desires;
dependent on the diversity of desires, there arises the diversity of fevers; dependent on the diversity of fevers, there arises the diversity of quests.
Dependent on diversity in search, there arises diversity in gain—these are the nine diversities.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom in the discernment of the nine ideas is knowledge of the diversity of ideas.
This is the nineteenth exposition: Knowledge of the Diversity of Ideas.

1.1.20–24 Exposition of the Fivefold Knowledge How is it that wisdom as direct knowledge is knowledge in the sense of having known; wisdom as full understanding is knowledge in the sense of investigating; wisdom as abandoning is knowledge in the sense of relinquishing; wisdom as development is knowledge in the sense of single flavor; and wisdom as realization is knowledge in the sense of touching?
Whatever states are directly known, those states are known.
Whatever phenomena have been fully understood, those phenomena have been scrutinized.
Whatever phenomena have been abandoned, those phenomena have been relinquished.
Whatever phenomena have been cultivated, those phenomena have a single flavor.
Whatever states have been realized, those same states have been touched.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:

“Wisdom as direct knowledge is knowledge in the sense of having known; wisdom as full understanding is knowledge in the sense of scrutinizing; wisdom as abandoning is knowledge in the sense of relinquishing; wisdom as development is knowledge in the sense of a single flavor; wisdom as realization is knowledge in the sense of contacting.
The twenty-fourth exposition: The Exposition of the Fivefold Knowledge. 1.1.25–28.
The Exposition of the Analytical Knowledges (*Paṭisambhidāñāṇaniddesa*).

How is it that wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning; wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena;
wisdom regarding the diversity of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language; and wisdom regarding the diversity of eloquence is knowledge of the analytical insight of eloquence?

The faculty of faith is a phenomenon (dhamma); the faculty of energy is a phenomenon; the faculty of mindfulness is a phenomenon; the faculty of concentration is a phenomenon; the faculty of wisdom is a phenomenon.
The faculty of faith is one thing, the faculty of energy is another, the faculty of mindfulness is another, the faculty of concentration is another, and the faculty of wisdom is another.
By whatever knowledge these various phenomena are known, by that very same knowledge they are fully realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
The meaning is the sense of resolution; the meaning is the sense of exertion; the meaning is the sense of establishment; the meaning is the sense of non-distraction;

the meaning is the sense of seeing. The meaning of resolution is one thing, the meaning of exertion is another, the meaning of establishment is another, the meaning of non-distraction is another, and the meaning of seeing is another.
"By whatever knowledge these various meanings are known, by that very same knowledge these various meanings are realized.
Therefore it is said: "Wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is the knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
There are expressions of phrasing and terminology to demonstrate five things; there are expressions of phrasing and terminology to demonstrate five meanings.
The linguistic expressions for phenomena are one thing, and the linguistic expressions for meanings are another.
By whatever knowledge these various linguistic expressions are known, by that very same knowledge these various linguistic expressions are fully realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
There are knowledges regarding five phenomena, knowledges regarding five meanings, and knowledges regarding ten linguistic expressions.
The knowledges regarding phenomena are distinct, the knowledges regarding meanings are distinct, and the knowledges regarding linguistic expressions are distinct.
By whatever knowledge these various knowledges were known, by that very same knowledge these various knowledges are realized.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom regarding the diversity of inspired ingenuity is the knowledge of the analytical insight of inspired ingenuity."
The power of faith is Dhamma; the power of energy is Dhamma; the power of mindfulness is Dhamma; the power of concentration is Dhamma;
the power of wisdom is Dhamma. The power of faith is one thing, the power of energy another, the power of mindfulness another, the power of concentration another, and the power of wisdom another.
By whatever knowledge these various phenomena are known, by that very same knowledge these various phenomena are fully realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Its meaning is the state of being unshakable by lack of faith.
The meaning is the state of being unshakable by laziness;
the meaning is the state of being unshakable by negligence;
the meaning is the state of being unshakable by restlessness.
The meaning of being unshakable by ignorance is one thing;

the meaning of being unshakable by lack of faith is another; the meaning of being unshakable by laziness is another; the meaning of being unshakable by negligence is another; the meaning of being unshakable by restlessness is another; and the meaning of being unshakable by ignorance is another.
By whatever knowledge these various meanings are known, by that very same knowledge these various meanings are fully realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
There are expressions of phrasing and terminology for the purpose of demonstrating five things; there are expressions of phrasing and terminology for the purpose of demonstrating five meanings.
The linguistic expressions for phenomena are one thing, and the linguistic expressions for meanings are another.
By whatever knowledge these various linguistic expressions are known, by that very same knowledge these various linguistic expressions are fully understood.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
There are knowledges regarding five phenomena, knowledges regarding five meanings, and knowledges regarding ten linguistic expressions.
The knowledges regarding phenomena are distinct, the knowledges regarding meanings are distinct, and the knowledges regarding linguistic expressions are distinct.”
By whatever knowledge these various knowledges are known, by that very same knowledge these various knowledges are realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of inspired ingenuity is the knowledge of the analytical insight of inspired ingenuity.”
The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is the Dhamma; the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena is the Dhamma;

the factor of enlightenment of energy is the Dhamma; the factor of enlightenment of rapture is the Dhamma; the factor of enlightenment of tranquility is the Dhamma; the factor of enlightenment of concentration is the Dhamma;
the factor of enlightenment of equanimity is the Dhamma.
The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is one thing; the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena is another;

the factor of enlightenment that is energy is another; the factor of enlightenment that is rapture is another; the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility is another; the factor of enlightenment that is concentration is another;
the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity is another.
By whatever knowledge these various phenomena were known, by that very same knowledge these various phenomena were realized.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is the knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā)."

The meaning of establishment is a meaning; the meaning of investigation is a meaning; the meaning of exertion is a meaning; the meaning of pervasion is a meaning; the meaning of tranquility is a meaning; the meaning of non-distraction is a meaning; the meaning of reflection is a meaning.

The meaning of establishment is one thing, the meaning of investigation is another, the meaning of exertion is another, the meaning of pervasion is another, the meaning of tranquility is another, the meaning of non-distraction is another, and the meaning of reflection is another.
By whatever knowledge these various meanings are known, by that same knowledge these various meanings are fully realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is knowledge of the discrimination of meaning.
There are expressions of phrasing and terminology to point out seven things; there are expressions of phrasing and terminology to point out seven meanings.
The linguistic expressions for phenomena are one thing, and the linguistic expressions for meanings are another.
By whatever knowledge these various linguistic expressions are known, by that very same knowledge these various linguistic expressions are fully realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
There are knowledges regarding seven phenomena, knowledges regarding seven meanings, and knowledges regarding fourteen modes of expression.
The knowledges regarding phenomena are distinct, the knowledges regarding meanings are distinct, and the knowledges regarding modes of expression are distinct.
By whatever knowledge these various knowledges are known, by that very same knowledge these various knowledges are realized.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom regarding the diversity of inspired eloquence is the knowledge of the analytical insight of inspired eloquence."

Right view is a state; right intention is a state; right speech is a state; right action is a state; right livelihood is a state; right effort is a state; right mindfulness is a state; right concentration is a state.
Right view as a state is one thing; right intention as a state is another; right speech as a state is another; right action as a state is another;
right livelihood as a state is another; right effort as a state is another; right mindfulness as a state is another; [right concentration as a state is another].
Right concentration is a Dhamma.
By means of that very same knowledge by which these various phenomena were known, they were also realized;
therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).

The meaning of seeing is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of directing onto is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of embracing is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of originating is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of purification is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of exertion is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of establishment is the meaning of purpose; the meaning of non-distraction is the meaning of purpose.
The meaning of seeing is one thing, the meaning of directing onto is another, the meaning of embracing is another, and...
The meaning of origination is one meaning; the meaning of cleansing is another meaning; the meaning of exertion is another meaning; the meaning of establishment is another meaning;
the meaning of non-distraction is another meaning.
By that very same knowledge by which these various meanings are known, these various meanings are also directly realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

These are the eight modes of expression through phonemes, etymologies, and utterances for the purpose of demonstrating the eight phenomena; these are the eight modes of expression through phonemes, etymologies, and utterances for the purpose of demonstrating the eight meanings.
The expressions for phenomena are one thing, and the expressions for meanings are another.
By whatever knowledge these various expressions are known, by that very same knowledge these various expressions are realized.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the diversity of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
There are knowledges regarding eight phenomena (dhamma), knowledges regarding eight meanings (attha), and knowledges regarding sixteen types of language.
The knowledges regarding phenomena are distinct, the knowledges regarding meanings are distinct, and the knowledges regarding language are distinct.
By whatever knowledge these various knowledges are known, by that very same knowledge these various knowledges are realized.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom regarding the diversity of inspired ingenuity is the knowledge of the analytical insight of inspired ingenuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa)."
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning."
Wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Wisdom regarding the diversity of expressions is knowledge of the analytical insight of expression (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
Wisdom regarding the diversity of ingenuity is knowledge of the analytical insight of ingenuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).
