The Exposition of the Threefold Knowledge How is it that wisdom regarding the diversity of abidings is knowledge of the meaning of abiding; wisdom regarding the diversity of attainments is knowledge of the meaning of attainment; and wisdom regarding the diversity of both abidings and attainments is knowledge of the meaning of both abiding and attainment?
Perceiving the sign as fearful, because of being intent upon the signless, one sees its passing away each time it arises—
this is the signless abiding. Perceiving aspiration as fearful, because of being intent upon the desireless, one sees its passing away each time it arises—
this is the desireless abiding.
Seeing obsession as fear, because of his inclination toward emptiness, he sees the passing away [of formations] whenever they arise—this is the dwelling in emptiness.

Seeing the sign as fear, because of his inclination toward the signless, he looks on with equanimity at the process of occurrence; having adverted to cessation, Nibbāna, which is signless, he attains it—this is the dwelling in the signless.

The signless attainment: seeing aspiration as fearful, because of being intent upon the wishless, one looks with equanimity upon the process [of existence], adverts to the cessation that is Nibbāna—the wishless—and attains it;
this is the wishless attainment.
Seeing misapprehension as fearful, because of being intent upon the void, one looks with equanimity upon the process [of existence], adverts to the cessation that is Nibbāna—the void—and attains it.
The attainment of emptiness (*suññatā-samāpatti*).

Seeing the sign as fearful, because of being intent upon the signless (*animitta*), one sees the passing away [of formations] each time they arise; having looked on with equanimity at their occurrence and having adverted to cessation, Nibbāna, which is signless, one attains it—this is the attainment of the dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra-samāpatti*).
Seeing aspiration (*paṇidhi*) as fearful, because of being intent upon the desireless (*appaṇihita*), one... [sees the passing away of formations each time they arise].

Having touched [the object], he sees its passing away; having looked on with equanimity at the process of occurrence, he adverts to cessation, Nibbāna, the wishless, and attains it—this is the attainment of the wishless abiding.

Seeing attachment as fearful and being inclined toward emptiness, he sees the passing away of each thing as he touches it; having looked on with equanimity at the process of occurrence, he adverts to cessation, Nibbāna, the empty, and attains it.
The attainment of the dwelling in emptiness.
Seeing the sign of form as fearful, because of being intent upon the signless, one sees its passing away each time it is contacted—
this is the dwelling in the signless.
Perceiving the aspiration for form as fearful, because he is intent upon the wishless, he sees its passing away as soon as it has arisen—
this is the wishless abiding. Perceiving misapprehension of form as fearful, because he is intent upon emptiness, he sees its passing away as soon as it has arisen— this is the empty abiding.
The void abiding.
Perceiving the sign of form as fearful, because of being intent upon the signless, he looks on with equanimity at what has arisen, adverts to cessation, Nibbāna, which is signless,
and attains it— the signless attainment.

Perceiving the aspiration for form as fearful, because he is intent upon the wishless, he looks on with equanimity at the process of existence, adverts to the wishless cessation that is Nibbāna, and attains it— this is the wishless attainment.

Perceiving adherence to form as fearful, because he is intent upon the void, he looks on with equanimity at the process of existence, adverts to the void cessation that is Nibbāna, and attains it— [this is the void attainment].
The attainment of emptiness (*suññatā-samāpatti*).

Perceiving the sign of form as fearful, because of being intent upon the signless (*animitta*), one sees the passing away of things as they are repeatedly encountered; having looked on with equanimity at the process of occurrence and having adverted to cessation, Nibbāna, which is signless, one attains it—this is the attainment of the dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra-samāpatti*).

Perceiving the aspiration for form as fearful, because he is intent upon the wishless, he sees its passing away each time it arises; having looked on with equanimity at its occurrence, he adverts to cessation, Nibbāna, the wishless, and attains it—this is the attainment of the wishless abiding.

Perceiving attachment to form as fearful, because he is intent upon the void, he sees its passing away each time it arises; having looked on with equanimity at its occurrence, he adverts to cessation, Nibbāna, the void, and attains it—[this is the attainment of the void abiding].
The attainment of the dwelling in emptiness.
The sign of feeling …pe… the sign of perception …
The sign of volitional formations … the sign of consciousness … the sign of the eye … [and so on] … up to … [the signs of the other sense bases].
Perceiving aging and death as a source of fear, because he is intent upon the signless (*animitta*), he sees their passing away again and again— this is the signless dwelling (*animittavihāra*).
Perceiving the longing for aging and death as a source of fear, because he is intent upon the wishless (*appaṇihita*), he sees their passing away again and again.
The wishless abiding.
Seeing attachment to aging and death as fearful, because of being intent upon emptiness, one sees their passing away as one repeatedly touches it—
the void abiding.

Perceiving the sign of aging and death as fearful, because he is intent upon the signless, he looks with equanimity upon the process of existence, adverts to cessation—that is, Nibbāna—the signless, and attains it:
this is the signless attainment (*animittā samāpatti*).

Perceiving the aspiration for aging and death as fearful, because he is intent upon the wishless, he looks with equanimity upon the process of existence, adverts to cessation—that is, Nibbāna—the wishless, and attains it.
The wishless attainment (*appaṇihitā samāpatti*).

Seeing attachment to aging and death as fearful, and because of being intent upon emptiness (*suññatā*), one disregards what is occurring, adverts to cessation—the emptiness that is Nibbāna—and attains it:
this is the emptiness attainment (*suññatā samāpatti*).

Perceiving the sign of aging and death as fearful, because he is intent upon the signless, he sees the passing away [of formations] again and again; having looked with equanimity at what has arisen, he adverts to and enters Nibbāna, the cessation that is signless—this is the attainment of the signless abiding.

Perceiving the aspiration for aging and death as fearful, because he is intent upon the wishless, he sees the passing away [of formations] again and again; having looked with equanimity at what has arisen, he adverts to and enters Nibbāna, the cessation that is wishless—this is the attainment of the wishless abiding.
The attainment of the dwelling in the wishless:

seeing the adherence to aging and death as fearful, because of being inclined toward emptiness, one sees their passing away each time they arise; having looked on with equanimity at the process of occurrence, one adverts to cessation, Nibbāna, as emptiness, and attains it—this is the attainment of the dwelling in emptiness.
The signless dwelling is one thing, the desireless dwelling is another, and the voidness dwelling is yet another.
The signless attainment is one thing, the desireless attainment is another, and the voidness attainment is yet another.
The signless dwelling-attainment is one thing, the desireless dwelling-attainment is another, and the voidness dwelling-attainment is yet another.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:

"Wisdom regarding the diversity of abidings is knowledge regarding the state of abiding; wisdom regarding the diversity of attainments is knowledge regarding the state of attainment; wisdom regarding the diversity of abidings and attainments is knowledge regarding the state of abiding and attainment."

Exposition of the Knowledge of Immediate Concentration.
How is it that wisdom regarding the cutting off of the taints through non-distraction and purification is knowledge of immediate concentration?
Through renunciation, one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind is concentration.
Through that concentration, knowledge arises.
By means of that knowledge, the taints are exhausted.
Thus, first comes serenity, afterwards knowledge.
By that knowledge there is the destruction of the taints.
Therefore it is said:
“Because of its purity through non-distraction, wisdom regarding the complete cutting off of the taints is knowledge of the concentration that is immediately followed by the fruit.
What are these taints?
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.
Where do these taints (āsavas) come to exhaustion?

By means of the stream-entry path (sotāpattimagga), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) is exhausted without remainder; the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) leading to states of deprivation is exhausted; the taint of existence (bhavāsava) leading to states of deprivation is exhausted; and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) leading to states of deprivation is exhausted.
It is here that these taints come to exhaustion.

By the path of once-returning, the gross taint of sensual desire is exhausted; the corresponding taint of existence is exhausted; the corresponding taint of ignorance is exhausted. It is here that these taints are exhausted.
By the path of non-returning, the taint of sensual desire is exhausted without remainder; the corresponding taint of existence is exhausted; the corresponding taint of ignorance is exhausted.
It is here that these taints are exhausted.
By means of the path of arahantship, the taint of existence is exhausted without remainder, and the taint of ignorance is exhausted without remainder.
It is here that these taints are exhausted.
