1.1.33. Exposition of Knowledge of the Abiding in Harmlessness:
How is it that wisdom—consisting in the predominance of vision, the attainment of peaceful abidings, and resolution upon the sublime—is knowledge of the abiding in harmlessness?
"Predominance of seeing": the contemplation of impermanence is predominance of seeing; the contemplation of suffering is predominance of seeing;
the contemplation of non-self is predominance of seeing. The contemplation of impermanence in regard to form is predominance of seeing;
the contemplation of suffering in regard to form is predominance of seeing; the contemplation of non-self in regard to form is predominance of seeing.
In feeling …pe… in perception … in volitional formations …

In consciousness … in the eye … [and so on] … in aging-and-death, the contemplation of impermanence has vision as its dominant influence; in aging-and-death, the contemplation of suffering has vision as its dominant influence; in aging-and-death, the contemplation of non-self has vision as its dominant influence.
And "the attainment of a peaceful dwelling" means: the dwelling in emptiness is the attainment of a peaceful dwelling;
the dwelling in the signless is the attainment of a peaceful dwelling;
the dwelling in the desireless is the attainment of a peaceful dwelling.
"Adherence to the sublime" means adherence to emptiness is adherence to the sublime;
adherence to the signless is adherence to the sublime;
adherence to the desireless is adherence to the sublime.
"Abiding in non-conflict": the first jhāna is abiding in non-conflict;
the second jhāna is abiding in non-conflict;
the third jhāna is abiding in non-conflict.
The fourth jhāna is an abiding in non-affliction.
The attainment of the base of infinite space is an abiding in non-affliction …pe… the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is an abiding in non-affliction.
What is the meaning of "dwelling in the absence of conflict" (*araṇavihāra*)?
It is called dwelling in the absence of conflict because, by means of the first jhāna, one removes the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Thus it is "dwelling in the absence of conflict."
By means of the second jhāna, one removes applied thought and sustained thought;
thus it is the "abiding in non-conflict.
By means of the third jhāna, one removes rapture; thus it is [the abiding in non-conflict].
The dwelling in freedom from conflict (*araṇavihāra*).
By means of the fourth jhāna, one removes pleasure and pain; thus it is called the dwelling in freedom from conflict.

The dwelling in non-affliction (*araṇavihāra*) consists in removing the perception of form, the perception of sensory reaction, and the perception of diversity by means of the attainment of the base of infinite space.
The dwelling in non-affliction consists in removing the perception of the base of infinite space by means of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness.

The dwelling in freedom from conflict (*araṇavihāra*). It is called the dwelling in freedom from conflict because, through the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti*), it removes the perception of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana-saññā*).
One removes the perception of the base of nothingness by means of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the dwelling in non-affliction (*araṇavihāra*). This is the dwelling in non-affliction.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom that has vision as its dominant factor, the attainment of peaceful abiding, and the inclination toward the sublime, is knowledge regarding the abiding in non-conflict."
The Thirty-third Exposition: Knowledge of Dwelling in the State Free from Conflict (Araṇavihārañāṇaniddesa). 1.1.34.

Exposition of Knowledge of the Attainment of Cessation (Nirodhasamāpattiñāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom consisting in mastery—by virtue of being endowed with two powers, the subsiding of three formations, sixteen modes of knowledge, and nine modes of concentration—is knowledge of the attainment of cessation?
"By two powers" means two powers:
the power of serenity and the power of insight.
What is the power of serenity?
One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction by means of renunciation is the power of serenity.
One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction by means of non-ill will is the power of serenity.
One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction by means of the perception of light is the power of serenity.
One-pointedness of mind through non-distraction is non-distraction, the power of serenity...
[and so on] ...one-pointedness of mind through non-distraction by way of breathing in while contemplating relinquishment is the power of serenity;
one-pointedness of mind through non-distraction by way of breathing out while contemplating relinquishment is the power of serenity.
In what sense is it the "power of serenity"?
Because it is not shaken by the hindrances through the first jhāna,
it is the power of serenity.
By means of the second jhāna, one is unshaken by applied and sustained thought;
this is the power of serenity.
By means of the third jhāna, one is unshaken by rapture; this is...
The power of serenity:
by means of the fourth jhāna, one is unshaken by pleasure and pain—
this is the power of serenity.
It does not waver from the attainment of the base of infinite space due to the perception of form, the perception of resistance, or the perception of diversity—
this is the power of serenity.
It does not waver from the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness due to the perception of the base of infinite space— this is the power of serenity.
The power of serenity.
It does not waver from the perception of the base of infinite consciousness when attaining the base of nothingness;
this is the power of serenity.
It does not waver from the perception of the base of nothingness regarding the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
this is the power of serenity (*samathabala*).
It does not waver, does not shake, and does not tremble from restlessness, from the defilements associated with restlessness, or from the aggregates: this is the power of insight (*vipassanābala*).
The power of serenity.
This is the power of serenity.
What is the power of insight?
Contemplation of impermanence is the power of insight;
contemplation of suffering is the power of insight;
contemplation of non-self is the power of insight.
Contemplation of disenchantment is the power of insight.
Contemplation of dispassion is the power of insight.
Contemplation of cessation is the power of insight.
The power of insight is the contemplation of relinquishment.
The power of insight is the contemplation of impermanence in form … [and so on] … the power of insight is the contemplation of relinquishment in form.
In feeling … perception … volitional formations … [he dwells contemplating impermanence, suffering, and non-self].
Contemplation of impermanence regarding consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … regarding aging-and-death is the power of insight … [and so on].
The power of insight is the contemplation of relinquishment regarding aging and death.
In what sense is it called the "power of insight"?
It is because it does not waver from the perception of permanence due to the contemplation of impermanence.
The power of insight.
It does not waver from the perception of pleasure when contemplating suffering—
this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from the perception of self due to the contemplation of non-self:
this is the power of insight.
It does not waver from delight due to the contemplation of disenchantment: this is the power of insight.
The power of insight.
Through the contemplation of dispassion, it does not waver in the face of lust—
this is the power of insight.
It does not waver regarding origination through the contemplation of cessation:
this is the power of insight.
It does not waver regarding grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment: this is the power of insight.
The power of insight.
It does not waver, does not shake, and does not tremble before ignorance and the defilements associated with ignorance, nor before the aggregates;
thus it is the power of insight.
This is the power of insight.
And "the subsiding of three formations": of which three formations is there subsiding?
For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied thought and sustained thought—the verbal formations—have subsided.
For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the bodily formations consisting of in-breaths and out-breaths are stilled.
For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, the mental formations consisting of perception and feeling are stilled.
It is through the stilling of these three formations [that this state is reached].
"By means of the sixteen modes of knowledge": by which sixteen modes of knowledge?

The mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of impermanence, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of suffering, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of non-self, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of disenchantment, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of dispassion, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of cessation, [the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of relinquishment, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of destruction, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of vanishing, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of fading away, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of cessation, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of letting go, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of the signless, the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of the desireless, and the mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of emptiness]."
The exercise of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of relinquishment; the exercise of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of turning away;
the path of stream-entry as an exercise of knowledge; the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry as an exercise of knowledge; the path of once-returning as an exercise of knowledge;

the attainment of the fruit of once-returning as an exercise of knowledge; the path of non-returning as an exercise of knowledge; the attainment of the fruit of non-returning as an exercise of knowledge; the path of arahantship...
The course of knowledge, the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, and the course of knowledge—
these are the sixteen courses of knowledge.
Regarding "by nine courses of concentration," by which nine courses of concentration?
The first jhāna is a practice of concentration; the second jhāna is a practice of concentration; the third jhāna is a practice of concentration; the fourth jhāna is a practice of concentration;
the attainment of the base of infinite space … [and so on] … the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness … the attainment of the base of nothingness …
The attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the practice of concentration.
For the sake of attaining the first jhāna, there is applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind; ...pe...
for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
By means of these nine modes of practice for concentration.
"Mastery" refers to the five masteries:
mastery in adverting, mastery in attaining, mastery in resolving, mastery in emerging, and mastery in reviewing.
One adverts to the first jhāna wherever, whenever, and for as long as one wishes;
there is no sluggishness in adverting—
this is mastery over adverting.
He enters the first jhāna wherever he wishes, whenever he wishes, and for as long as he wishes;
there is no sluggishness in entering it—
this is mastery in entering.
One resolves upon the first jhāna wherever one wishes, in whatever way one wishes, and for as long as one wishes;
there is no sluggishness in this resolution—
this is mastery over resolution.
The first jhāna emerges wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes;
there is no sluggishness in emerging—
this is mastery over emergence.
He reviews the first jhāna wherever, whenever, and for as long as he wishes;
there is no sluggishness in his reviewing—
this is mastery in reviewing.
He adverts to the second jhāna …pe… to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception whenever he wishes, in whatever way he wishes, and for as long as he wishes;
there is no sluggishness in his adverting— thus it is.
Mastery over adverting:
he enters upon the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception whenever, in whatever way, and for as long as he wishes; ... pe ...
he resolves.
He emerges ...
he reviews; there is no sluggishness in his reviewing—thus...
The mastery of reviewing.
These are the five masteries.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:

"Wisdom that has mastery through two powers, through the subsiding of three formations, and through sixteen modes of knowledge and nine modes of concentration, is the knowledge of the attainment of cessation.
This concludes the forty-fourth exposition: the Knowledge of the Attainment of Cessation.
1.1.35. Exposition of the Knowledge of Parinibbāna How is it that wisdom regarding the exhaustion of the occurrence of one who is clearly comprehending is knowledge of parinibbāna?
Here, one who is clearly comprehending exhausts the occurrence of sensual desire through renunciation, and the occurrence of ill will through non-ill will.
One exhausts the occurrence of sloth and torpor by means of the perception of light; one exhausts the occurrence of restlessness by means of non-distraction;
one exhausts the occurrence of doubt by means of the discernment of phenomena; ... and so on ... one exhausts ignorance by means of knowledge.
Through gladness, discontent is exhausted;
through the first jhāna, the occurrence of the hindrances is exhausted; ... pe ...
through the path of arahantship, the occurrence of all defilements is exhausted.
Alternatively, for one who is fully conscious and attaining final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue, this very process of the eye ceases and no other process of the eye arises;
this very process of the ear … [and so on] … this very process of the nose ceases.
He brings to an end the activity of the tongue,
the activity of the body,
and the activity of the mind, and no further activity of the mind arises.
This wisdom regarding the exhaustion of what has occurred for one who is clearly comprehending is knowledge of final Nibbāna.
It is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is called:
“Wisdom regarding the exhaustion of what has occurred for one who is clearly comprehending is knowledge of final Nibbāna.
This is the thirty-fifth exposition: the Exposition of Knowledge of Final Nibbāna. 1.1.36.
The Exposition of Knowledge of the Meaning of the Level Head.
How is it that wisdom regarding the right cutting off, cessation, and non-reappearance of all phenomena is knowledge of the meaning of the "even-headedness"?
"All phenomena" refers to:

the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements; wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena; phenomena of the sense sphere, phenomena of the fine-material sphere, phenomena of the immaterial sphere, and phenomena not included [in the mundane spheres].
One completely eradicates: through renunciation, one completely eradicates sensual desire;
through non-ill will, one completely eradicates ill will;
through the perception of light, one completely eradicates sloth and torpor.
By means of non-distraction, one completely eradicates restlessness.
By means of the discernment of phenomena, one completely eradicates doubt.
By means of knowledge, one completely eradicates ignorance.
Through joy, one completely eradicates discontent.
Through the first jhāna, one completely eradicates the hindrances...
[and so on] ...through the path of arahantship, one completely eradicates all defilements.
He causes cessation: he causes the cessation of sensual desire through renunciation;
he causes the cessation of ill will through non-ill will;
he causes the cessation of sloth and torpor through the perception of light.
Through non-distraction, one ceases restlessness.
Through the discernment of phenomena, one ceases doubt.
Through knowledge, one ceases ignorance.
Through gladness, one ceases discontent.
Through the first jhāna, one ceases the hindrances … [and so on] … through the path of arahantship, one ceases all defilements.
Non-appearance means that for one who has attained renunciation, sensual desire does not appear;
for one who has attained non-ill will, ill will does not appear;
for one who has attained the perception of light, sloth and torpor do not appear.
For one who has attained non-distraction, restlessness does not arise.
For one who has attained the discernment of phenomena, doubt does not arise.
For one who has attained knowledge, ignorance does not arise.
Discontent does not arise for one who has attained gladness.
The hindrances do not arise for one who has attained the first jhāna … [and so on] … all defilements do not arise for one who has attained the path of arahantship.
Equanimity is equanimity through the abandoning of sensual desire;
non-ill will is equanimity through the abandoning of ill will;
perception of light is equanimity through the abandoning of sloth and torpor.
Due to the abandoning of restlessness, non-distraction is balanced.
Due to the abandoning of doubt, the discernment of phenomena is balanced.
Due to the abandoning of ignorance, knowledge is balanced.
Because of the abandoning of discontent, joy is even.
Because of the abandoning of the hindrances, the first jhāna is even … [and so on] … because of the abandoning of all defilements, the path of arahantship is even.
“Summits” refers to thirteen summits: the summit of craving, which is an impediment; the summit of conceit, which is a bond; the summit of views, which is misapprehension;
the summit of agitation, which is restlessness; the summit of defilement, which is ignorance; the summit of resolution, which is faith; and the summit of exertion, which is energy.
Mindfulness has the headship of establishment; concentration has the headship of non-distraction; wisdom has the headship of seeing; the life-faculty has the headship of occurrence;
liberation has the headship of the range; and cessation has the headship of formations.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing, and wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
"The wisdom regarding the complete cutting off and the non-reappearance of all phenomena in their cessation is knowledge in the sense of an even-headedness.
This is the thirty-sixth exposition: Knowledge in the Sense of an Even-Headedness.
1.1.37. Exposition of the Knowledge of the Meaning of Effacement How is it that wisdom regarding the exhaustion of various and diverse fires is knowledge of the meaning of effacement?
"Various" means:
Lust is manifold, hatred is manifold, delusion is manifold; anger … [and so on] … resentment … contempt … [and so on].
...malice...
envy...
avarice...
Deceit … guile … obstinacy …
Aggression … conceit … overweening pride …
Intoxication … negligence … all defilements …
All misconducts… all volitional formations… all kamma leading to existence.
"Multiplicity and unity": sensual desire is multiplicity, renunciation is unity.
Ill will is multiplicity, non-ill will is unity.
Sloth and torpor are multiplicity, the perception of light is unity.
Restlessness is diversity; non-distraction is unity.
Doubt is diversity; the discernment of phenomena is unity.
Ignorance is diversity; knowledge is unity.
Discontent is diversity; joy is unity.
The hindrances are diversity; the first jhāna is unity … [and so on] … All defilements are diversity; the path of arahantship is unity.
There are five kinds of radiance:
the radiance of conduct, the radiance of virtue, the radiance of wisdom, the radiance of merit, and the radiance of the Dhamma.
Because it is ignited by the radiance of conduct, it consumes the radiance of immorality.
Because it is ignited by the fire of virtue, it consumes the fire of non-virtue.
Because it is ignited by the fire of wisdom, it consumes the fire of lack of wisdom.
Because it is ignited by the fire of merit, it consumes the fire of demerit.
Because it is sharpened by the power of the Dhamma, it consumes the power of non-Dhamma.
"Effacement" (sallekha): sensual desire is non-effacement; renunciation is effacement.
Ill will is non-effacement; non-ill will is effacement.
Lethargy and drowsiness are non-effacement; perception of light is effacement.
Restlessness is non-effacement; non-distraction is effacement.
Doubt is non-effacement; the discernment of phenomena is effacement.
Ignorance is non-effacement; knowledge is effacement.
Discontent is non-effacement; gladness is effacement.
The hindrances are non-effacement; the first jhāna is effacement ... [and so on] ...
All defilements are non-effacement; the path of arahantship is effacement.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the exhaustion of the various distinct fires is knowledge in the sense of effacement.
This is the thirty-seventh instruction on the knowledge of the sense of effacement.
1.1.38 The Instruction on the Knowledge of Arousal of Energy.
What is the knowledge of the arousal of energy regarding the meaning of non-laxity and resolute exertion?
Wisdom regarding the meaning of non-laxity and resolute exertion for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
Wisdom regarding the meaning of non-laxity and resolute exertion for the sake of the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
Wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of exertion and resolute determination for the arising of unarisen wholesome states is knowledge of the arousal of energy.

Wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of exertion and resolute determination for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
Wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of exertion and resolute determination for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
Wisdom regarding the state of non-laziness and resolute exertion for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
Wisdom regarding the state of non-laziness and resolute exertion for the arising of unarisen renunciation is knowledge of the arousal of energy.

Wisdom regarding the state of non-laziness and resolute exertion for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen renunciation is knowledge of the arousal of energy …pe….
Wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of exertion and resoluteness for the non-arising of all unarisen defilements is knowledge of the application of energy.

Wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of exertion and resoluteness for the abandoning of all arisen defilements is knowledge of the application of energy …pe… wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of exertion and resoluteness for the arising of the unarisen path of arahantship is knowledge of the application of energy.

Wisdom regarding the application of energy in the sense of non-laziness and resolute exertion for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of the arisen path of arahantship is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; wisdom in the sense of understanding. Therefore, it is called: [knowledge of the arousal of energy].
“Wisdom regarding the meaning of non-laxity, self-exertion, and striving is knowledge of the arousal of energy.
This is the fortieth instruction: the exposition of the knowledge of the arousal of energy. 1.1.39.
Exposition of the Knowledge of the Demonstration of Meaning.
How is it that wisdom as the manifestation of various phenomena is knowledge in the demonstration of meaning?
"Various phenomena" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena,
indeterminate phenomena, sense-sphere phenomena, fine-material-sphere phenomena, and immaterial-sphere phenomena.
Unincluded states.
"Expounding" means: one expounds material form as impermanent, expounds material form as suffering, expounds material form as non-self.
Feeling ... [and so on] ... [as above].
perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
He reveals the eye...
[and so on] ... as impermanent; he reveals aging-and-death as suffering; he reveals aging-and-death as non-self.
In "the demonstration of the goal," by abandoning sensual desire, he demonstrates the goal of renunciation.
By abandoning ill will, he demonstrates the purpose of non-ill will.
By abandoning sloth and torpor, he demonstrates the purpose of the perception of light.
By abandoning restlessness, he demonstrates the purpose of non-distraction.
Abandoning doubt, he demonstrates for the purpose of defining the Dhamma.
Abandoning ignorance, he demonstrates for the purpose of knowledge.
Abandoning aversion, he demonstrates for the purpose of gladness.
While abandoning the hindrances, it demonstrates the purpose of the first jhāna; ... pe ...
while abandoning all defilements, it demonstrates the purpose of the path to arahantship.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge (ñāṇa); in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom (paññā).
Therefore it is said:
"Wisdom as the manifestation of various phenomena is knowledge in the demonstration of the goal.
This is the ninetieth chapter: The Exposition of Knowledge in the Demonstration of the Goal.

1.1.40. Exposition of the Knowledge of Purification by Vision How is it that wisdom regarding the penetration of the inclusion of all phenomena under a single category, their diversity, and their unity, is the knowledge of purification by vision?
"Of all phenomena" refers to the five aggregates … [and so forth] … [as previously detailed].
Unincluded states.

By a single inclusion: all phenomena are included as one by way of twelve aspects—by way of the sense of suchness, the sense of non-self, the sense of truth, the sense of penetration, the sense of higher knowledge, and the sense of full understanding.

In the sense of the Dhamma, in the sense of the element, in the sense of the known, in the sense of realization, in the sense of touching, and in the sense of convergence—in these twelve aspects, all phenomena are comprised as one.
As for "diversity and unity": sensual desire is diversity, renunciation is unity; ... [and so on] ...
All defilements are diversity; the path of arahantship is unity.
"Penetrates" means he penetrates the truth of suffering through the penetration of full understanding;
he penetrates the truth of the origin through the penetration of abandoning.
One penetrates the truth of cessation through the penetration of realization.
One penetrates the truth of the path through the penetration of development.
Regarding "purification by vision": at the moment of the stream-entry path, vision becomes purified.
At the moment of the fruit of stream-entry, vision is purified.
At the moment of the path of once-returning, vision is being purified;
at the moment of the fruit of once-returning, vision is purified.
At the moment of the path of non-returning, vision is purified;
at the moment of the fruit of non-returning, vision is purified.
At the moment of the path of arahantship, vision is purified.
At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, vision is purified.
That is knowledge in the sense of having known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the penetration of the unity, diversity, and oneness of all phenomena is the knowledge of purification by vision.
This is the fortieth chapter: the Exposition of the Knowledge of Purification by Vision. 1.1.41.
The Exposition of the Knowledge of Acceptance.
How is it that wisdom through the state of having known is knowledge of acceptance?
Form is known as impermanent; form is known as suffering; form is known as non-self.
Whatever is known, that is accepted. Thus, wisdom through the state of having known is knowledge of acceptance.
Wisdom as the state of having known is the knowledge of patience.
Feeling … perception … [and so on] … [the same applies to the other aggregates].
Volitional formations … consciousness … the eye … [and so on] … [the six sense bases] … contact … feeling … craving … clinging … becoming … birth … aging-and-death.
Aging-and-death is known as impermanent; aging-and-death is known as suffering; aging-and-death is known as non-self.
Whatever is known, that is approved of—thus, wisdom through the state of being known is the knowledge of approval (*khantiñāṇa*).
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
"Because of having understood, wisdom is the knowledge of acceptance."
The fortieth chapter: The Exposition of the Knowledge of Patience.
The forty-first chapter: The Exposition of the Knowledge of Thorough Penetration.
How is it that wisdom, through its contact [with the object], is the knowledge of thorough penetration?
One touches form as impermanent, one touches form as suffering, one touches form as non-self.
Whatever one touches, that one thoroughly investigates— thus,
wisdom through contact is knowledge of thorough investigation.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations … [and so on] … consciousness.
He touches consciousness ... the eye ...
and so on ... aging-and-death as impermanent, he touches it as suffering, he touches it as non-self.
"Whatever it touches, that it thoroughly grasps"— thus,
wisdom is knowledge through its state of having touched;
it is knowledge in the sense of knowing, and wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom, through having touched [the object], is knowledge of fathoming.
This is the forty-second exposition on the knowledge of fathoming.
1.1.43. Exposition of the Knowledge of Abiding in a Portion (Padesavihārañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom in synthesis is knowledge of abiding in a portion?
There is feeling conditioned by wrong view, and there is also feeling conditioned by the subsiding of wrong view.
There is feeling conditioned by right view, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of right view.
There is feeling conditioned by wrong intention, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of wrong intention.
There is feeling conditioned by right intention, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of right intention... [and so on] ...
There is feeling conditioned by wrong liberation, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of wrong liberation.
There is feeling conditioned by right liberation, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of right liberation.
There is feeling conditioned by desire, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of desire.
There is feeling conditioned by applied thought, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of applied thought.
There is feeling conditioned by perception, and there is feeling conditioned by the subsiding of perception.
When desire is not subsided, and applied thought is not subsided, and perception is not subsided, there is feeling conditioned by that as well.
Desire has subsided, but applied thought has not subsided, and perception has not subsided; there is feeling conditioned by that.
Desire has subsided, and applied thought has subsided, but perception has not subsided; there is feeling conditioned by that.
Desire has subsided, and applied thought has subsided, and perception has subsided; there is feeling conditioned by that.
For the attainment of what has not yet been attained there is effort; when that state has been reached, there is feeling conditioned by it.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing, and wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, this is called:
“Wisdom regarding integration is knowledge regarding partial dwelling.
This is the forty-third exposition: the Exposition of Knowledge Regarding Partial Dwelling. 1.1.44–49:
The Exposition of Knowledge Regarding the Turning of the Skin.
How is it that wisdom, through its predominance, is knowledge of the turning away from perception?
Because of the predominance of renunciation, wisdom turns away from perception due to sensual desire;
thus, wisdom, through its predominance, is knowledge of the turning away from perception.
Because of the predominance of non-ill will, wisdom turns away from ill will through perception;
thus, "wisdom due to predominance" is knowledge of the turning away of perception.
Because of the predominance of the perception of light, wisdom turns away from sloth and torpor through perception; thus—
Because it has predominance, wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception.
Because it has non-distraction as its predominance, wisdom turns away from agitation through perception;
thus, because it has predominance, wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception.
Because of the predominance of the discernment of phenomena, wisdom turns away from the perception of doubt;
thus, because of its predominance, wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception. Because of the predominance of knowledge, wisdom turns away from the perception of ignorance; thus—
Because it has predominance, wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception.
Because it has gladness as its predominance, wisdom turns away from the perception of discontent;
thus, because it has predominance, wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception.
Because of its predominance over the first jhāna, wisdom turns away from perception due to the hindrances— thus, because of its predominance,

wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception … pe … because of its predominance over the path of arahantship, wisdom turns away from perception due to all defilements— thus, because of its predominance, wisdom is knowledge of the turning away from perception.
Through its predominance, wisdom is knowledge regarding the turning away from perception.
That is knowledge in the sense of having known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
“Because it is predominant, wisdom regarding the turning away from perception is knowledge.
How is it that wisdom regarding diversity is knowledge of the turning away of the mind?
Sensual desire is diversity; renunciation is unity.
When one intends for unity through renunciation, the mind turns away from sensual desire;
thus, wisdom regarding diversity is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
Ill will is diversity; non-ill will is unity.
When one intends unification amidst non-ill-will, the mind turns away from ill-will:
thus, wisdom regarding diversity is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
Sloth and torpor are diversity; perception of light is unification.
"One who intends unification through the perception of light turns the mind away from sloth and torpor"—this is wisdom regarding diversity as knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
…pe… All defilements are diversity; the path of arahantship is unity.
When one intends the state of being a single factor of the path to arahantship, the mind turns away from all defilements;
thus, wisdom regarding diversity is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding diversity is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
How is wisdom regarding resolution knowledge of the turning away of the mind?
"Abandoning sensual desire, one resolves the mind by means of renunciation"—
this wisdom regarding resolution is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
"Abandoning ill will, one resolves the mind by means of non-ill will"— [this wisdom regarding resolution is knowledge of the turning away of the mind].
Wisdom regarding resolution is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
One who abandons sloth and torpor resolves the mind by means of the perception of light;
thus, wisdom regarding resolution is knowledge of the turning away of the mind …pe…
One who abandons all defilements resolves the mind by means of the path of arahantship;
thus, wisdom regarding resolution is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
In the sense of knowing it is knowledge, in the sense of understanding it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding resolution is knowledge of the turning away of the mind.
How is wisdom regarding emptiness knowledge of the turning away of knowledge?

“Eye is empty of self or of what belongs to self, of permanence, of stability, of eternalism, or of a state that does not change”—for one who knows and sees this as it really is, knowledge turns away from misapprehension regarding the eye;
thus, wisdom regarding emptiness is knowledge of the turning away of knowledge.
“Ear is empty …” [and so on].
The nose is empty...
the tongue is empty...
the body is empty...

“Mind is empty of a self, or of what belongs to a self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternalism, or of a nature that does not change”—for one who thus knows and sees according to reality, knowledge turns away from mental misapprehension;
this is wisdom regarding emptiness as knowledge of turning away.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding emptiness is knowledge of the turning away through knowledge.
How is it that wisdom regarding relinquishment is knowledge of the turning away through liberation?
“By means of renunciation, one relinquishes sensual desire”—

this is wisdom regarding relinquishment, knowledge regarding the turning away from liberation. “By means of non-ill will, one relinquishes ill will”— this is wisdom regarding relinquishment, knowledge regarding the turning away from liberation.
Wisdom regarding relinquishment is knowledge of the turning away through liberation.
One relinquishes sloth and torpor by means of the perception of light;
thus, wisdom regarding relinquishment is knowledge of the turning away through liberation.
"By means of non-distraction, one relinquishes restlessness"—

this wisdom in relinquishment is knowledge of the turning away through liberation. "By means of the definition of phenomena, one relinquishes doubt"— this wisdom in relinquishment is knowledge of the turning away through liberation.
Wisdom regarding relinquishment is knowledge of turning away through liberation:
… [as before] … by means of the path of arahantship, one relinquishes all defilements—
this is wisdom regarding relinquishment, knowledge of turning away through liberation.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom in relinquishment is knowledge in the turning away through liberation.”
How is it that wisdom regarding the meaning of suchness is knowledge of the turning away from the truths?
One who fully understands suffering’s meaning of oppression, its meaning of being conditioned, its meaning of burning, and its meaning of change, turns away;
thus, wisdom regarding the meaning of suchness is knowledge of the turning away from the truths.
"Turning away by abandoning the origin's meaning of accumulation, its meaning of source, its meaning of bondage, and its meaning of obstruction"—this is wisdom regarding the state of suchness;
it is knowledge of turning away from the truth.

"Turning away by realizing cessation's meaning of escape, its meaning of seclusion, its meaning of the unconditioned, and its meaning of the deathless"—[this is wisdom regarding the state of suchness; it is knowledge of turning away from the truth]."
Wisdom regarding the state of suchness is knowledge of the turning away from the truths.
By developing the path’s sense of outlet, its sense of cause, its sense of seeing, and its sense of predominance, one turns away;
thus, wisdom regarding the state of suchness is knowledge of the turning away from the truths.
The turning away through perception, the turning away through mind, the turning away through consciousness, the turning away through knowledge, the turning away through liberation,
and the turning away through truth. One turns away while perceiving— thus it is the turning away through perception.
It turns away while intending, thus it is the turning away of mind (cetovivaṭṭa).
It turns away while cognizing, thus it is...
The turning away of the mind is *cittavivaṭṭa*. Turning away by exercising knowledge is *ñāṇavivaṭṭa*.
Turning away while relinquishing is the turning away of liberation (*vimokkhavivaṭṭa*). Turning away in the sense of suchness (*tathaṭṭha*) is the turning away of suchness (*tathatā-vivaṭṭa*).
The turning away from truth.
Where there is the turning away from perception, there is the turning away of the mind;
where there is the turning away of the mind, there is the turning away from perception.
Where there is the turning away from perception and the turning away of the mind, there is the turning away of consciousness.
Where there is the turning away of consciousness, there is the turning away from perception and the turning away of the mind.
Where there is the turning away from perception, the turning away of the mind, and the turning away of consciousness, there is the turning away through knowledge.
Where there is the turning away through knowledge, there is the turning away through perception, the turning away through mind, and the turning away through consciousness.

Where there is the turning away through perception, the turning away through mind, the turning away through consciousness, and the turning away through knowledge, there is the turning away through liberation.

Where there is the turning away through liberation, there is the turning away through perception, the turning away through mind, the turning away through consciousness, and the turning away through knowledge.

Where there is the turning away from perception, the turning away of the mind, the turning away of consciousness, the turning away through knowledge, and the turning away through liberation, there is the turning away from truth.

Where there is the turning away from truth, there is the turning away from perception, the turning away of the mind, the turning away of consciousness, the turning away through knowledge, and the turning away through liberation.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom regarding the state of suchness is knowledge of the turning away from the truths.
This is the forty-ninth exposition: the description of the knowledge of the turning away from the corpse.

1.1.50. Exposition of the Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Power (Iddhividhañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom regarding the sense of success in the meaning of succeeding—by means of resolution, through the singleness of both body and mind, and through the perception of ease and the perception of lightness—is knowledge of the modes of supernormal power?

Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis for supernormal power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for supernormal power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving... [and so on].

He develops the basis for psychic power; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
He thoroughly cultivates, thoroughly disciplines, makes pliant, and renders wieldy his mind in these four bases for psychic power.
Having thoroughly cultivated, thoroughly disciplined, made pliant, and rendered wieldy his mind in these four bases for psychic power...
He absorbs the body into the mind, and he absorbs the mind into the body; he transforms the mind according to the body, and he transforms the body according to the mind;
he resolves upon the mind by means of the body, and he resolves upon the body by means of the mind.

Having transformed the mind according to the body and having transformed the body according to the mind, and having resolved upon the mind by means of the body and having resolved upon the body by means of the mind, he dwells having entered upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness in the body.
Thus, with a mind so developed, purified, and cleansed, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).
He experiences manifold supernormal powers:
having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one.
He appears and disappears;
he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space;
and he dives in and out of the earth, as if in water.
He walks on water without sinking, just as on solid ground;
he travels through the air cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
and with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so powerful and majestic.
He exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is called:

“Wisdom regarding the meaning of success through the basis of determination—consisting in the single-pointedness of both body and mind, and the perception of pleasure and lightness—is knowledge of the modes of supernormal power.
This is the fiftieth chapter: the Exposition of Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Power. 1.1.51. Exposition of Knowledge of the Purity of the Divine Ear Element.
How is it that wisdom in the thorough penetration of various and manifold sounds and signs by means of the expansion of applied thought is the knowledge of the purification of the ear-element?
Here, a bhikkhu [attains] concentration through desire … pe … concentration through energy … [and so on].

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
He thoroughly cultivates and thoroughly tames his mind in these four bases for psychic power, making it pliant and wieldy.
Thus, having cultivated and thoroughly tamed the mind with respect to these four bases of psychic power, making it pliant and workable, he attends to the sound-sign of sounds even at a distance;
he attends to the sound-sign of sounds even nearby; he attends to the sound-sign of gross sounds as well as subtle sounds.
He attends to the sign of sound; he attends to the sign of sound even of very subtle sounds;
he attends to the sign of sound in the eastern direction, he attends to the sign of sound in the western direction, and he attends to the sign of sound in the northern direction.
He attends to the sign of sound among sounds in the southern direction; he attends to the sign of sound among sounds in the southeastern intermediate direction;
he attends to the sign of sound among sounds in the southwestern intermediate direction;
he attends to the sign of sound among sounds in the northern intermediate direction; and he attends to the sign of sound among sounds in the southern intermediate direction.
He attends to the sign of sound from sounds in the intermediate direction; he attends to the sign of sound from sounds in the lower direction;
he attends to the sign of sound from sounds in the upper direction.
With his mind thus developed, purified, and cleansed, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the purification of the ear-element.
Thus, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, one hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
“Wisdom that, by means of the expansion of applied thought, thoroughly penetrates the various and single sounds and signs, is the knowledge of the purification of the ear element.
This is the fifty-first exposition: the description of the knowledge of the purification of the ear element.

1.1.52. Exposition of the Knowledge of Penetrating Others’ Minds (Cetopariyañāṇaniddesa) How is it that wisdom in fathoming the course of consciousness—whether diverse or uniform—by means of the clarity of the faculties due to the expansion of three types of consciousness is the knowledge of penetrating others’ minds?

Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through desire and the volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through energy … [and so on].

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving … pe … he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
He thoroughly trains his mind in these four bases for psychic power, thoroughly disciplines it, makes it pliant, and makes it wieldy.
Thus, having fully developed and thoroughly tamed the mind in these four bases for psychic power, making it pliant and wieldy, he understands thus:
"This form is originated by the faculty of joy; this form is originated by the faculty of grief; this form is originated by the faculty of equanimity.
With his mind thus developed, purified, and cleansed, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of others' minds.
Thus, having encompassed with his own mind the minds of other beings and other individuals,
he understands: he understands a mind affected by lust as "a mind affected by lust," and he understands a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust."
A mind with hatred … [and so on] … a mind free from hatred … a mind with delusion … [and so on] … a mind free from delusion …
a mind free from delusion … a contracted mind … a scattered mind …
or a developed mind … or an undeveloped mind … or a surpassable mind …
Whether the mind is unsurpassed … or concentrated … or unconcentrated …
Or, when the mind is liberated, he understands the liberated mind as "the liberated mind"; or when the mind is unliberated, he understands the unliberated mind as "the unliberated mind.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore it is said:

“Understanding that, by means of the clarity of the faculties due to the expansion of three kinds of consciousness, fathoms the course of consciousness in its diversity and unity, is knowledge of penetration of minds.
The Exposition of Knowledge of Penetration of Minds is the fifty-second.

1.1.53. Exposition of the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives How is it that wisdom in the thorough penetration of phenomena as they proceed by way of conditions—by means of the diverse and manifold expansion of kamma—is the knowledge of recollection of past lives?
Here, a bhikkhu, through the concentration gained by desire … [and so forth] … [the rest of the formula].
Having made it pliant and workable, he understands thus:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises—namely, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition..."
The six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises;
conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises;
and conditioned by birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
“Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
With his mind thus developed, purified, and cleansed, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say:
One birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births,
forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births,
a hundred thousand births; many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both contraction and expansion.
Regarding the aeons of dissolution and evolution:

"In such a place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I arose in another place.
There too I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here."
Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and details.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, this is called:
“Wisdom that thoroughly penetrates conditioned phenomena as they arise through the power of the diverse and manifold diffusion of kamma is the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
This concludes the fifty-third exposition: the Exposition of the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives. 1.1.54.
The Exposition of the Knowledge of the Divine Eye.
How is it that wisdom regarding the seeing of signs of forms—both diverse and uniform—by means of illumination is the knowledge of the divine eye?

Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through desire and the volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through energy … pe … he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through mind … pe …
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
He thoroughly cultivates, thoroughly disciplines, makes pliant, and makes his mind workable in these four bases for psychic power.

Having thoroughly cultivated, thoroughly disciplined, made pliant, and made his mind workable in these four bases for psychic power, he attends to the perception of light and resolves upon the perception of day.
“As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a luminous mind.
With his mind thus developed—purified and cleansed—he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:

"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind; they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong view."
"Upon the dissolution of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation,

a bad destination, perdition, even in hell. But these worthy beings, having been endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind, not reviling the noble ones, holding right view,
and undertaking actions based on right view— upon the dissolution of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, even in a heavenly world."

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore, it is called:
“Wisdom in the sense of seeing signs of various and single forms by means of illumination is the knowledge of the divine eye.
This is the fifty-fourth exposition: the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Divine Eye. 1.1.55.
The Exposition of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints.
And how is it that wisdom as mastery over the three faculties in sixty-four modes is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints?
Which three faculties?
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known.

To how many bases does the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" go? To how many bases does the faculty of final knowledge go? To how many bases does the faculty of one who has already known go?
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" goes to one base:
the path of stream-entry.
The faculty of final knowledge proceeds to six states:
the fruit of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the fruit of once-returning, the path of non-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the path of arahantship.
The faculty of one who has already known proceeds to one state: [the fruit of arahantship].
The fruit of arahantship.
At the moment of the stream-entry path, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" has the faculty of faith as its accompaniment of resolution;
the faculty of energy has the accompaniment of exertion; the faculty of mindfulness has the accompaniment of establishment; and the faculty of concentration...
The faculty of non-distraction has non-distraction as its retinue; the faculty of wisdom has seeing as its retinue; the faculty of mind has cognizing as its retinue;
the faculty of mental pleasure has moistening as its retinue; the life-faculty has the predominance of the continuity of occurrence as its retinue.
At the moment of the stream-entry path, all states that have arisen—excluding mind-produced matter—are exclusively wholesome.
All are free from taints; all are conducive to liberation; all lead to the diminution [of defilements];
all are supramundane; all have Nibbāna as their object.
At the moment of the path of stream-entry, these eight faculties are the co-nascent attendants of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
They are mutual attendants, they are attendants by way of support, they are attendants by way of association,
they are co-existent, they are conascent, they are conjoined, and they are associated.
These very factors are both its modes and its attendants.

At the moment of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) has resolution as its accompaniment; the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) has exertion as its accompaniment;
the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) has establishment as its accompaniment; the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) has non-distraction as its accompaniment;

the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) has seeing as its accompaniment; the faculty of mind (manindriya) has cognizing as its accompaniment; and the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) [has gladness as its accompaniment].
It has intention as its concomitant; the life-faculty has the continuity of the process of existence as its dominant influence and concomitant.

At the moment of the fruit of stream-entry, all phenomena that have arisen are indeterminate (*avyākata*); with the exception of mind-originated matter, they are all free from taints (*anāsava*), all are supramundane (*lokuttara*), and all have Nibbāna as their object.
At the moment of the fruit of stream-entry, these eight faculties are the co-nascent concomitants of the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*), and they are mutual concomitants.
They are its supports, its attendants, its associated attendants; they are co-existent, conascent, conjoined, and associated.
These very factors are both its modes and its attendants.
At the moment of the path of once-returning …pe… at the moment of the fruit of once-returning …pe… at the moment of the path of non-returning …pe…
At the moment of the fruit of non-returning …pe… at the moment of the path to arahantship,
for the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is its retinue of resolve;
…pe… the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is its retinue governed by the continuity of the process of existence.
At the moment of the path of arahantship, all phenomena born therein— excluding mind-produced matter—
are exclusively wholesome, exclusively free from taints, exclusively leading to liberation, exclusively conducive to the waning of existence,
exclusively supramundane, and exclusively have Nibbāna as their object.
At the moment of the path of Arahatship, these eight faculties are the companions of the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) by way of co-nascence, mutual assistance,
support, and association; they are conascent, co-existent, conjoined, and associated.
These are both its modes and its concomitants.

At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, the faculty of final knowledge (aññātāvindriya) has the faculty of faith as its concomitant of resolution, the faculty of energy as its concomitant of exertion,
the faculty of mindfulness as its concomitant of establishment, and the faculty of concentration as its concomitant of non-distraction.

The faith faculty has confidence as its retinue; the energy faculty has exertion as its retinue; the mindfulness faculty has non-forgetfulness as its retinue; the concentration faculty has non-distraction as its retinue;

the wisdom faculty has seeing as its retinue; the mind faculty has cognizing as its retinue; the joy faculty has suffusing as its retinue; and the life faculty has the predominance of the continuity of occurrence as its retinue.

At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, all the states that have arisen are exclusively indeterminate; with the exception of mind-produced matter, all are entirely without taints, all are supramundane, and all have Nibbāna as their object.
At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, these eight faculties are the companions of the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) by way of co-nascence, mutual assistance,
support, and association; they are conascent, co-arisen, conjoined, and associated.
These very same are its modes (*ākāra*) and its attendants (*parivāra*).
Thus, these eight groups of eight make sixty-four.
What are these "taints" (*āsava*)? Which taints are they?
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.
Where do these taints come to exhaustion?

By means of the stream-entry path, the taint of views is exhausted without remainder; the taint of sensual desire leading to states of deprivation is exhausted; the taint of existence leading to states of deprivation is exhausted; and the taint of ignorance leading to states of deprivation is exhausted.
Herein these taints are exhausted.
By means of the path of once-returning, the gross taint of sensual desire is exhausted; the corresponding taint of existence is exhausted; the corresponding taint of ignorance is exhausted.
Herein these taints are exhausted.

By the path of non-returning, the taint of sensual desire is exhausted without remainder; the taint of existence associated with it is exhausted; and the taint of ignorance associated with it is exhausted.
It is here that these taints are exhausted.
By the path of arahantship, the taint of existence is exhausted without remainder, and the taint of ignorance is exhausted without remainder.
Herein, these taints are exhausted.
In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom.
Therefore, it is said:
“Wisdom as mastery over the three faculties in sixty-four aspects is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
This concludes the fifty-fifth section: The Exposition of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints. 1.1.56–63: The Exposition of the Two Tetrad-Groups of Knowledge of the Truths.

How is it that wisdom regarding the meaning of full understanding is knowledge of suffering; wisdom regarding the meaning of abandoning is knowledge of the origin; wisdom regarding the meaning of realization is knowledge of cessation; and wisdom regarding the meaning of development is knowledge of the path?
The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of changeability, and the meaning of full understanding.
The meaning of the origin is accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, the meaning of obstruction, and the meaning of abandoning.
Cessation has the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, the meaning of the deathless, and the meaning of realization;
the path has the meaning of outlet, the meaning of cause, the meaning of seeing, the meaning of predominance, and the meaning of development.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:

“Wisdom in the sense of full understanding is knowledge regarding suffering; wisdom in the sense of abandoning is knowledge regarding its origin; wisdom in the sense of realizing is knowledge regarding its cessation; wisdom in the sense of developing is knowledge regarding the path.
How is there knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?

The knowledge of one possessing the path is knowledge regarding suffering, it is knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, it is knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and it is knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is knowledge regarding suffering?
It is the wisdom that arises with reference to suffering—understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment, and observation.
Discernment, close examination, sagacity, skill, subtlety, discrimination, reflection, investigation, vast intelligence, guidance, insight,
clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom,
the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view.
This is called knowledge regarding suffering.
With reference to the origin of suffering …pe… with reference to the cessation of suffering …pe…

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises with reference to the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—this is called knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
That is knowledge in the sense of knowing; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:
“Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is the sixty-seventh exposition: the two tetrads on the knowledge of the truths.

1.1.64–67 Exposition of the Knowledge of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidāñāṇaniddesa) What is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), knowledge of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), knowledge of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and knowledge of the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā)?

Knowledge regarding meanings is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge regarding phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena; knowledge regarding languages is the analytical knowledge of language; knowledge regarding ingenuity is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity.
Wisdom regarding the diversity of meaning is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning; wisdom regarding the diversity of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena;
wisdom regarding the diversity of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language; wisdom regarding the diversity of ingenuity is knowledge of the analytical insight of ingenuity;
wisdom in the discernment of meaning is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning; wisdom in the discernment of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena.
Wisdom in the discernment of language is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of language; wisdom in the discernment of perspicuity is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity.
Wisdom in the observation of meaning is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meaning; wisdom in the observation of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of phenomena.

Wisdom in the discernment of knowledge is the knowledge of the analytical insight of knowledge; wisdom in the discernment of language is the knowledge of the analytical insight of language; wisdom in the discernment of expression is the knowledge of the analytical insight of expression.
Wisdom in the discernment of meaning is the knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning; wisdom in the discernment of phenomena is the knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena.

Wisdom characterized by language is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*); wisdom characterized by ingenuity is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*).

Wisdom regarding the differentiation of meaning is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*); wisdom regarding the differentiation of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*).

Wisdom regarding the classification of knowledge is the knowledge of the analytical insight of knowledge (*ñāṇa-paṭisambhidā*); wisdom regarding the classification of language is the knowledge of the analytical insight of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*);

wisdom regarding the classification of eloquence is the knowledge of the analytical insight of eloquence (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). Wisdom in the elucidation of meaning is the knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*);

wisdom in the elucidation of phenomena is the knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*); wisdom in the elucidation of language is the knowledge of the analytical insight of language; wisdom in the elucidation of eloquence is...

Knowledge regarding the analytical knowledge of perspicuity is wisdom. Wisdom that illuminates meaning is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meaning; wisdom that illuminates the Dhamma is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma;
wisdom that illuminates language is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of language; wisdom that illuminates perspicuity is knowledge of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity.
Wisdom regarding the radiance of meaning is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning; wisdom regarding the radiance of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena;
wisdom regarding the radiance of language is knowledge of the analytical insight of language; wisdom regarding the radiance of ingenuity is knowledge of the analytical insight of ingenuity.
Wisdom regarding the elucidation of meaning is knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning; wisdom regarding the elucidation of phenomena is knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena.

Wisdom regarding the elucidation of knowledge is the knowledge of the analytical power of knowledge; wisdom regarding the elucidation of expression is the knowledge of the analytical power of expression; wisdom regarding the elucidation of ingenuity is the knowledge of the analytical power of ingenuity.
That is "knowledge" in the sense of having known, and "wisdom" in the sense of understanding.
Therefore it is said:

"Knowledge of the analytical insight of meaning, knowledge of the analytical insight of phenomena, knowledge of the analytical insight of language, and knowledge of the analytical insight of ingenuity.
This concludes the sixty-seventh exposition: the Exposition of Pure Analytical Insight Knowledge.

1.1.68. Exposition of the Knowledge of the Relative Superiority and Inferiority of the Faculties (Indriyaparopariyattañāṇaniddesa) What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the relative superiority and inferiority of the faculties?

Here, the Tathāgata sees beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, those of good disposition and... [those of bad disposition].
There are two types of persons: those who are easy to instruct and those who are difficult to instruct;
some who see fear in the other world and in wrongdoing, and some who do not see fear in the other world and in wrongdoing.
One with little dust in one's eyes is a person of faith; one with much dust in one's eyes is a person lacking faith.
A person who has aroused energy has little dust in their eyes; a person who is lazy has much dust in their eyes.
A person who is established in mindfulness has little dust in their eyes; a person who is muddled in mindfulness has much dust in their eyes.
A person who is concentrated has little dust in their eyes; a person who is unconcentrated has much dust in their eyes.
A person possessing wisdom has little dust in their eyes; a person lacking wisdom has much dust in their eyes.
Regarding those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties: a person endowed with faith has sharp faculties, while a person devoid of faith has dull faculties.
A person who has aroused energy has sharp faculties, while a person who is indolent has dull faculties.
A person who possesses established mindfulness has keen faculties; a person who possesses muddled mindfulness has dull faculties.
A person who is concentrated has keen faculties; a person who is unconcentrated has dull faculties.
A person who is wise has keen faculties; a person who is unwise has dull faculties.
Regarding "good appearance" and "bad appearance": a person who has faith is of good appearance; a person who lacks faith is of bad appearance.
A person who has aroused energy is of good appearance; a person who is lazy is of bad appearance.
A person whose mindfulness is established is of good appearance; a person who is muddled in mindfulness is of bad appearance.
A person who is concentrated is of good character; a person who is unconcentrated is of bad character.
A person who possesses wisdom is of good character; a person who lacks wisdom is of bad character.
Regarding "easy to instruct" and "difficult to instruct": a person endowed with faith is easy to instruct; a person devoid of faith is difficult to instruct.
A person who has aroused energy is easy to instruct; a person who is indolent is difficult to instruct.
A person who is established in mindfulness is easy to instruct; a person who is muddled in mindfulness is difficult to instruct.
A person who is concentrated is easy to instruct; a person who is unconcentrated is difficult to instruct.
A person possessed of wisdom is easy to instruct, while a person lacking wisdom is difficult to instruct.

Some perceive the fear of blame regarding the world beyond, while others do not perceive the fear of blame regarding the world beyond. A person of faith perceives the fear of blame regarding the world beyond, whereas a person lacking faith does not perceive the fear of blame regarding the world beyond.
A person who has aroused energy perceives the fear of blame regarding the world beyond, whereas a person who is lazy does not perceive the fear of blame regarding the world beyond.
A person established in mindfulness sees the fear of blame and the next world; a person of muddled mindfulness does not see the fear of blame and the next world.
A person concentrated sees the fear of blame and the next world; a person unconcentrated does not see the fear of blame and the next world.
A person possessing wisdom sees the fear of blame and the next world; a person of poor wisdom does not see the fear of blame and the next world.

1.1.69. The Exposition of the Knowledge of Dispositions and Latent Tendencies.
What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the dispositions and latent tendencies of beings?

Here, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of beings, he knows their underlying tendencies, he knows their conduct, he knows their dispositions, and he discerns beings who are capable and those who are incapable.
What is the inclination of beings?
It is either: "The world is eternal," or "The world is not eternal," or "The world is finite," or "The world is infinite."

or "that the soul is the same as the body," or "the soul is one thing and the body another," or "a Tathāgata exists after death," or "a Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death."
Thus, beings are either dependent upon the view of existence or dependent upon the view of non-existence.

But by not approaching either of these two extremes, there arises an acceptance in accordance with reality or knowledge as it truly is regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination.
