This is the underlying disposition of beings.
And what is the underlying tendency of beings? The underlying tendencies of beings are:

the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable, therein the underlying tendency to sensual lust lies latent in beings.
Whatever in the world is unpleasant and disagreeable, therein the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in beings.
Thus, ignorance underlies these two states; and pride, views, and doubt, which are associated with it, should likewise be regarded as underlying them.
This is the underlying tendency of beings.
And what is the conduct of beings?
It is the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable; whether belonging to a limited sphere or a vast sphere.
This is the conduct of beings.
And what is the inclination of beings?
There are beings with inferior inclinations; there are beings with superior inclinations.
Beings of inferior inclination associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings of inferior inclination.
Beings of superior inclination associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings of superior inclination.
In the past, too, beings of inferior inclination associated with, frequented, and attended upon beings of inferior inclination.
Beings who are inclined toward the sublime associated with beings who are inclined toward the sublime; they served them, frequented them, and attended upon them.
In the future as well, beings who are inclined toward the inferior will serve, frequent, and attend upon beings who are inclined toward the inferior;
beings who are inclined toward the sublime will serve, frequent, and attend upon beings who are inclined toward the sublime.
This is the disposition of beings.
Which beings are incapable?

Those beings who are possessed of an obstruction of karma, possessed of an obstruction of defilements, possessed of an obstruction of ripening; who lack faith, lack desire [for the good], and lack wisdom; who are incapable of entering into the certainty of the rightness of wholesome states.
These beings are incapable.
Which beings are capable?
Those beings who are not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karma, not possessed of an obstruction consisting of defilements, and not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karmic result.
Endowed with faith, zealous, and possessed of wisdom, they are capable of entering into the certainty of correctness regarding wholesome states—
these are beings who are capable.
This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings.

Great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
as they behold [the world]. Seeing that the dwelling of the world is obsessed by the sixty-two views,
great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
I have crossed over, while the world has not crossed over; I am liberated, while the world is not liberated;
I am tamed, while the world is untamed;
I am at peace, while the world is not at peace.
I am comforted, yet the world is not comforted;
I have attained final Nibbāna, yet the world has not attained final Nibbāna.

I am indeed able—having crossed over, to help others cross; being liberated, to liberate others; being tamed, to tame others; being at peace, to bring others to peace; being comforted, to comfort others; having attained final Nibbāna, to lead others to final Nibbāna.
Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they pass by sentient beings.
This is the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s attainment of great compassion.
This is the seventieth-first exposition on the knowledge of great compassion.
1.1.72–73 Description of Omniscient Knowledge:
What is the Tathāgata’s omniscient knowledge?
It is that which knows all the conditioned and the unconditioned without exception. Thus it is called omniscient knowledge.
It is the knowledge of omniscience.
Because there is no obstruction therein,
it is "unobstructed knowledge" (anāvaraṇañāṇa).
It knows all that is past—
this is omniscient knowledge.

Unobstructed knowledge.

"The Tathāgata is therefore called 'the one with the universal eye' (samantacakkhu).
In what sense is he "the one with the universal eye"?
It is in the sense of the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha.
Knowledge of suffering is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the origin of suffering is Buddha-knowledge;

knowledge of the cessation of suffering is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the analytical insight into meaning is Buddha-knowledge;

knowledge of the analytical insight into phenomena is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the analytical insight into language is Buddha-knowledge; [knowledge of the analytical insight into eloquence is Buddha-knowledge].
Knowledge is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings is Buddha-knowledge;
knowledge of the Twin Miracle is Buddha-knowledge; knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is Buddha-knowledge;
omniscient knowledge is Buddha-knowledge; unobstructed knowledge is Buddha-knowledge.
These are the fourteen types of Buddha-knowledge.
Of these fourteen types of Buddha-knowledge, eight are shared with disciples;
six are not shared with disciples.
To the extent that the meaning of suffering as suffering is all known,
and there is no meaning of suffering unknown—
this is omniscient knowledge.
In this regard, "there is no obstruction" refers to unobstructed knowledge.
To whatever extent there is the meaning of suffering in suffering, all that is known, all seen, all understood, all realized, and all touched by wisdom.
That there is no state of suffering untouched by wisdom—
this is omniscient knowledge. That therein there is no obstruction— this is omniscient knowledge.
Unobstructed knowledge:
as far as the meaning of origination regarding origination...
as far as the meaning of cessation regarding cessation...

To the extent that there is the state of being the path in the path …pe… to the extent that there is the state of analytical knowledge of meaning in the analytical knowledge of meaning … to the extent that there is the state of analytical knowledge of phenomena in the analytical knowledge of phenomena …
To the extent that there is the meaning of the analytical knowledge of language in the analytical knowledge of language...

to the extent that there is the meaning of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity in the analytical knowledge of perspicuity—all that is known, all seen, all understood, all realized, and all touched by wisdom.
There is no meaning of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity in the analytical knowledge of perspicuity that has not been touched by wisdom.
It is the knowledge of omniscience.
Since there is no obstruction therein,
it is unobstructed knowledge.

It is the knowledge of omniscience.
Since there is no obstruction therein,
it is "unobstructed knowledge."

To the extent that there is anything seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or examined by the mind in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans— all that is known, all that is seen,

There is nothing here that he has not seen,

The Tathāgata has directly known everything that is to be known;
therefore, he is the All-Seeing One.
